notes: These are the visions (literally The vision): This term introduces the book as a unified whole, covering Isaiah’s prophecies over a period of some fifty-five years (about 740–685 BC). • Isaiah son of Amoz: Beyond this, nothing is known of Isaiah’s family background. • Jerusalem, the capital city of Judah, was the center of Isaiah’s ministry. However, some of his prophecies also relate to the northern kingdom, Israel (referred to as Samaria and Ephraim, Isaiah 9:8-21; Isaiah 28:1-13), which fell in 722 BC (see 2 Kgs 17).
heavens . . . earth: All of creation is called to witness the trial that God convened against Judah (cp. Deuteronomy 31:28; Deuteronomy 32:1).
an ox knows its owner: Not so with Judah. Yet despite their rebellion, God still graciously addressed them as my people.

The expression Holy One of Israel is frequently used in Isaiah as a title for the Lord. God is the righteous and just King of heaven and earth (Isaiah 6:3-5), the incomparable God (Isaiah 40:25), and the Redeemer of his people (Isaiah 43:14). It was a terrible and foolish sin for Judah to reject him.

God sent famine, war, disease, and death as punishment. In most cases, however, God wanted to change stubborn behavior rather than simply to punish. • As a result of their persistent rebellion, the people’s head is injured and their heart is sick. The nation was wounded physically from Assyrian aggression, while spiritually they were defiled and overtaken by sin (Isaiah 64:6).
without any soothing ointments or bandages: Judah’s national condition was like the body of an injured person who had not received medical care.

country . . . towns: By 701 BC, the Assyrians had destroyed the infrastructure, taken cities, and ravaged the fields (see Isaiah 64:10). This fulfilled Isaiah’s prophetic word (Isaiah 6:11-13). Those who survived this Assyrian onslaught would know by experience to heed later warnings of exile to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6-7). God does what he says he will do, so the warning of God’s judgment on all the nations is certain.

Beautiful Jerusalem (Hebrew The daughter of Zion): Zion, one of the hills on which Jerusalem stands, often served as a synonym for Jerusalem. Zion carried with it the notion of God’s presence (Psalm 46:1-11), his protection of his people, and Jerusalem’s resistance to enemy forces. Now, however, the opposite was true. Jerusalem had become weak, like a helpless city under siege and like an abandoned . . . shelter or lean-to.

The Lord of Heaven’s Armies refers to the millions of angels that are at the Lord’s command (see 2 Kgs 6:16-17; Matthew 26:53). At the Exodus, Moses described God as a warrior fighting for his people (Exodus 15:1-21). Ironically, in Isaiah’s day, God fought against Judah because of their wickedness (Isaiah 1:24; Isaiah 3:1-5).

Listen to (literally listen to the word of) the Lord: In this context, listen means to respond in obedience to the law (or teaching; Hebrew torah) of our God (see Isaiah 2:3; Isaiah 5:24). • leaders . . . people: All levels of society were guilty. • Like Sodom and Gomorrah, Jerusalem had come under divine judgment for its rebellion against God’s laws. Jerusalem might have been utterly destroyed like those cities were it not for God’s grace (Isaiah 1:9; see Genesis 19:1-38).

The people had so offended God through their sin that he took no pleasure any more in their sacrifices. The Lord wanted Judah to stop the religious exercises he had commanded them to do rather than to continue them in a manner that was sinful and false (Isaiah 1:13). Ritual is never an acceptable substitute for true godliness.

The incense that accompanied offerings was intended as a sweet fragrance to the Lord (see Exodus 30:7-8), but when offered with hypocrisy it was a nauseating stench and an abomination to God. • While the Lord had ordered special days for fasting at the Temple (Leviticus 16:31; Leviticus 23:32; Numbers 29:7), they were ruined by the guilt of Judah’s sin (see Isaiah 58:1-7; Matthew 6:16-18). • pious meetings: These holy days were associated with the new moon and other festivals (see Leviticus 23:1-44).

New moon celebrations occurred on the first day of each lunar month (Numbers 28:11-15) and included sacrifices, feasting, and rest from work. • The annual festivals were the festivals of Passover, Harvest, Trumpets, and Shelters (Numbers 28:16–29:39; Deuteronomy 16:1-17).

I will not look . . . I will not listen: The Lord does not respond to prayer offered from a life of persistent wickedness. In this case, God charged the people with perverting his laws in order to practice violent injustice toward innocent victims.

Wash . . . and be clean! The people were defiled by their sin and the uncleanness of their sacrifices. To be clean in God’s eyes, they needed to change their behavior, get rid of their sins, and give up their evil ways (see also Isaiah 1:18).

Seeking justice means upholding God’s standards of fairness and advancing the rights of the oppressed, orphans, and widows—those who are weak and marginalized in society (see also Jeremiah 7:5-7; Jeremiah 22:3; Zechariah 7:10; Matthew 23:23; Matthew 25:31-46; James 1:27).

God called his people to come and settle their dispute so that he could restore his covenant relationship with them. This required Judah to make a decision between obeying or turning away (Isaiah 1:19-20). Isaiah says their sins are like scarlet . . . they are red like crimson, the color of blood, which Judah had unjustly shed (Isaiah 1:15). • white as snow . . . white as wool: The people would be radically transformed—cleansed, purified, and made holy (see also Psalm 51:7; Daniel 7:9).
Repentance leads to life, whereas resisting God’s will and turning away from him results in death (see Deuteronomy 11:26-28; Deuteronomy 28:1-62).
I, the Lord, have spoken! This statement marks the solemnity of what God has just promised. The phrase is used eleven times in Isaiah.
The image of Jerusalem as a prostitute represents Judah’s unfaithfulness to God (see Jeremiah 3:6-14; Ezekiel 16:25-26; Hosea 1:1–3:5).

The Lord of Heaven’s Armies, the Mighty One of Israel, was usually Israel’s protector (Isaiah 31:5). However, in this context, God was coming to take revenge against his own people, who by their wickedness had become his enemies and foes.

I will raise my fist against you: God, normally Israel’s protector, would become their attacker. However, he had a purpose beyond punishment. • I will melt you down. . . . I will remove all your impurities: God would use the Exile to remove the wicked from among his people and to refine those who would return.

The restoration of the community would be marked by new leaders who uphold justice rather than perverting it (see Isaiah 1:23). Jerusalem would again be pure silver (see Isaiah 1:22), the Home of Justice and the Faithful City.

Here, Zion refers to the remnant community. Only those who repent would receive God’s salvation and purification and would dwell in his presence. Zion was required to be the bastion of justice and righteousness, for God loves righteousness. God expected the covenant community to reflect the holy standards he cares about.

The rebels (Isaiah 1:28), who practiced idolatry in groves of sacred oaks and in gardens dedicated to idols, would become like drought-stricken oaks and gardens. They would lack the nourishing vitality of the true God’s presence. Those who followed the Canaanite fertility religion of Baal treated gardens and trees as sacred, believing that they brought blessings. Instead, they brought spiritual death.

vision (literally word): This heading (see Isaiah 1:1) likely introduces the revelation of chs Isaiah 2:1–12:6. The main focus of this section is on Judah, but a handful of passages expand that focus to include the nations in general (Isaiah 2:2-4), humanity at large (Isaiah 2:6-22), Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel (chs Isaiah 7:1–9:21), and the Assyrians (ch Isaiah 10:1-34).

In the Old Testament, the expression the last days is a general reference to the future era (see Jeremiah 49:39; Ezekiel 38:16; Hosea 3:5); in the New Testament, it is used to refer to the period that began with the coming of the Lord Jesus (Hebrews 1:2) and more specifically to the period immediately preceding the end of the present age (2 Pet 3:3). • The mountain of the Lord’s house referred to the Temple Mount. This location symbolized God’s glorious exaltation (see Isaiah 6:1) and his kingdom on earth. Isaiah’s focus on God’s exalted and supreme kingship flows out of his famous vision of God (ch Isaiah 6:1-13). • Far from being a narrow nationalistic dream, Isaiah’s prophetic hope extended beyond Judah and Jerusalem to include people from all over the world.

God’s gracious salvation would one day extend beyond Israel and Judah. This would prompt the nations to come to Zion, not in battle but to be blessed there and live by the rules of God’s kingdom. Isaiah encouraged Judah to look at the benefits that the nations would enjoy. He wanted to stimulate the people of Judah (Isaiah 2:5) to jealousy and provoke them to follow the Lord so that they would not be left out in that day. This section is repeated almost verbatim in Micah 4:1-3.

Human society will undergo changes as people conform to God’s revelation and follow his ways and paths. • Judah received the revelation (teaching . . . word) but did not obey it (Isaiah 1:10-15); however, the nations will be ready to do God’s will.

The Kingdom of God is evident when conflict and violence end, and it is characterized by peace (Romans 14:17). People will cooperate willingly or they will be forced to end their hostilities (Psalm 46:9). The nations will submit to divine arbitration rather than go to war (see Isaiah 1:18-20). • The words mediate and settle refer to God’s acts here, but later verses show the Messiah as the executor of justice (Isaiah 11:3-4). When this takes place, war will cease, and the nations will change their instruments of war into agricultural tools. • swords into plowshares: Cp. Joel 3:10, where the nations are exhorted to hammer their plowshares into swords.

Come . . . let us walk: Walking in God’s light (his revelation) will lead to glorious participation in his kingdom (see Isaiah 60:1; 1 Jn 1:7). God is the only light that overcomes the darkness of sin and evil (Isaiah 9:2). People cannot generate such light in and of themselves (Isaiah 59:9) but must walk in the light God provides, as they trust him and live in obedience to his will (Isaiah 50:10). • The phrase descendants of Jacob alludes to Israel’s special historic relationship with the Lord as well as their history of sinfulness and rebellion (see Isaiah 14:1; Isaiah 48:1).

The prophet threatened judgment and scoffed at human pride. All human structures (religious, economic, military, social) will come under divine scrutiny and be found deficient on the day of the Lord—that final day in history when God will judge the wicked once and for all (1 Cor 1:8; 1 Thes 5:2; 2 Thes 2:2; 2 Pet 3:10; Revelation 20:7-15). At times, the prophets also used the expression “the day of the Lord” (or others like it, such as “that day”) to refer to special instances of God’s judgment upon wickedness during the course of history (see Isaiah 13:6, Isaiah 13:9; Ezekiel 13:5; Ezekiel 30:3; Obadiah 1:15). On the day of the Lord, God alone will be exalted, while all human wickedness and pride will be struck down. The glorious day of God’s coming will fill wicked and arrogant humans with terror (Isaiah 2:10, Isaiah 2:19, Isaiah 2:21).
Isaiah condemned Israel’s and Judah’s arrogance and self-exaltation, warning them that only God was to be exalted. All attempts by humans to lift themselves up will actually result in humiliation.

The Lord had rejected his people to discipline them (Isaiah 8:17). While not permanent, the rejection seriously threatened their expectations of a glorious future. • sorcerers: These practitioners of pagan religion were expressly banned from Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). • The Philistines were Israel’s ancient enemies (Isaiah 9:12; Isaiah 11:14; Isaiah 14:29, Isaiah 14:31).

Isaiah pointed out all the things that people substitute for the true God: material achievements and securities (silver . . . treasures), military strength (warhorses . . . chariots), and objects of affection (idols). Such wealth and military strength characterized the reign of King Uzziah (2 Chr 26:6-21). Elsewhere, Isaiah pointed out the sheer folly of worshiping anything that is made with one’s own hands (see Isaiah 44:9-20; Isaiah 45:16).

In the day of God’s judgment, people will seek refuge in caves in the rocks, natural hiding places in the rocky land of Judah, rather than repent in humility before almighty God. Kings and leaders as well as slaves and free persons will seek protection from judgment (see also Revelation 6:15). • The terror of the Lord refers to God’s unbridled wrath against wickedness that will be revealed on the day of the Lord’s judgment. The prophecy shifts from Israel (Isaiah 2:5-6) to humanity at large. The Lord is against anything and anyone that exalts and trusts in human structures and beliefs rather than in him (Isaiah 2:11-12, Isaiah 2:22).

A key theme in Isaiah is that the Lord will be exalted and humble people will be restored (Isaiah 57:15), while proud and mighty people are humbled (Isaiah 26:5). • The day of judgment and the “day of reckoning” are also called the “day of the Lord.” There are seven such references in chs Isaiah 2:1–4:6 (Isaiah 2:11, Isaiah 2:17, Isaiah 2:20; Isaiah 3:6, Isaiah 3:18; Isaiah 4:1, Isaiah 4:2).

The cedars of Lebanon were prized trees used in the construction of Solomon’s Temple and palace (1 Kgs 5:6) and other important buildings (Ezra 3:7). They represented wealth and power (2 Chr 25:18; Psalm 92:12; Psalm 104:16), yet these mighty trees were as nothing before the Lord (Isaiah 10:34; Isaiah 33:9; see the boast of Sennacherib in Isaiah 37:24). • The oaks of Bashan were also an image of strength and splendor (Ezekiel 27:6); they, too, will disappoint (Isaiah 33:9; Nahum 1:4; Zechariah 11:2).
The prophet used several images of human strength to elaborate on Isaiah 2:11-12.
every magnificent vessel: Ornate sea-going vessels were a sign of prosperity.
The day of judgment is the “day of the Lord” (see Isaiah 13:4-13).
Animals such as rodents and bats lead a shadowy, subterranean existence. Those who worship idols will become like them in attempting to escape the Lord’s judgment.

The judgment prophecy of Isaiah 2:6-21 is set between two related exhortations: to trust the Lord (Isaiah 2:5) and not to put trust in human beings (Isaiah 2:22). • Human strength is temporary, frail as breath (see Psalm 90:1-17).
take away . . . bread . . . water: God had long ago warned of famine, with its horrible conditions that sometimes led to desperate acts, as one possible judgment for wickedness (Leviticus 26:26-29).

These verses continue the subject of judgment against Israel’s leadership (see Isaiah 1:23-25). The removal of leadership at all levels would allow the mob to gain control. Chaos and famine would turn Judah and Jerusalem into a social wasteland.

Regardless of their status, all military, civil, judicial, and religious leaders would be removed in the day of judgment (Isaiah 39:7; 2 Kgs 24:14-16). God would eventually give his people good leaders again (Isaiah 1:26) but not diviners and others who used pagan forms of revelation (Isaiah 47:9, Isaiah 47:12-13; see Deuteronomy 18:10-12).

Conditions would be so severe that boys and toddlers would qualify as candidates for office. By this, Isaiah either meant that adult leaders would be so decimated that only children would be left alive to assume the role or simply that the new leaders would be as immature, unwise, strong willed, and inexperienced as children.

Things would be so bad (a heap of ruins) that no one would want to take leadership. The people would become so desperate that anyone providing food or clothes (Isaiah 3:7) could be the leader of the people. In fact, however, no one would have food or clothing (see Isaiah 4:1).

The failure of human strength and societal organization can be a form of divine judgment. • to his face: The people of Judah had become bold in their wickedness like the people of Sodom (Isaiah 3:9; see also Isaiah 1:9-10).
The very look on their faces: At this time people boldly displayed their rebellion against God.
The godly—the righteous remnant—will receive God’s rewards (see Isaiah 40:10).
The wicked who practice and execute injustice will receive God’s just punishment.
The Lord is both the prosecutor and the supreme judge in this trial against his people.

elders and rulers: Wickedness and abuse by ungodly and incompetent leadership thwarts God’s purpose for his people (see also Isaiah 3:12). Therefore, leaders come under more severe judgment because they bear responsibility for the welfare of those under them. • my vineyard: See the Song of the Vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7).

The Lord cares for the poor. These were the marginalized and oppressed (see Isaiah 1:17), but God is their protector (see Isaiah 25:4). God called for his people to share his concern for the poor, but the Israelites were exploiting them to gain wealth (see Isaiah 3:14).

The dramatic descriptions show how the people of Jerusalem loved their refined way of life. They openly displayed their proud self-reliance, power, and prestige. • Beautiful Zion: See “Zion” Theme Note.

This passage applies the prophet’s teaching on arrogance (see Isaiah 2:11-12) to the people of Jerusalem. An alternate understanding is that this passage applies specifically to the women of Jerusalem.

In a reversal of fortune, the affluent and proud people of Jerusalem would suffer disgrace. Some of their ornaments (Isaiah 3:18) likely were amulets to keep evil away, but they could not ward off the calamity of judgment. These items of beauty were status symbols and represented financial security.
The men . . . will die in battle: Part of the city’s hopeless destitution would be the deaths of the men.

During Isaiah’s ministry, Jerusalem’s population was so decimated through war, famine, and disease (Isaiah 3:1-3; Isaiah 6:13; Isaiah 14:30; Isaiah 22:2; Isaiah 37:4) that there were few men left, creating an absence of leadership (see Isaiah 3:1-12). Even worse conditions lay ahead with the approaching war between Judah and the alliance of Syria and Israel in 734–732 BC (2 Chr 28) and eventually the conquest and fall of Jerusalem (605–586 BC).

The branch in this context probably refers to the remnant that would constitute Israel’s new beginning after the Exile (see Isaiah 6:13). Some also understand it as representing the ideal descendant of David, the Messiah (see Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15-16; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12). • A beautiful and glorious transformation from shame and disgrace (Isaiah 3:17-25) to fertility and beauty would manifest God’s presence and blessing among the remnant (Isaiah 4:6). • The fruit of the land, nature itself, would also be transformed from desolation to glory. Elsewhere, Isaiah described the future circumstances as resembling the Garden of Eden (see Isaiah 51:3; Isaiah 65:22). The message of renewal finds its ultimate fulfillment in the new creation (see Romans 8:19-27; 2 Cor 5:17; Galatians 6:15; Ephesians 2:15; Ephesians 4:24; Revelation 21:22-27). • Those who survive in Israel—the remnant—would be the true citizens of Zion.

In bold contrast to the desperate picture of Isaiah 3:16–4:1, this prophecy of salvation and hope (see also Isaiah 2:2-4) promised cleansing, consecration, and the renewal of God’s presence with the remnant. The imagery in Isaiah 4:5-6 alludes to Israel’s exodus from Egypt, when a pillar of cloud and of fire guided and protected them. Israel’s restoration from exile would be a second exodus.

To be holy was the requirement for citizenship in Zion, where God dwells in his glorious majesty (see Isaiah 6:3; Hebrews 12:14). • The remnant would have their names recorded among the living in the Book of Life (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:12).
God’s judgment has a purifying effect on his covenant people (see Malachi 3:3). Justice must be satisfied before restoration can be offered.
The references to a canopy of cloud . . . and smoke and flaming fire recall God’s continuous presence and protection during the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 13:21-22; Exodus 14:21-22).
shelter (literally shadow; see Isaiah 32:2): See Isaiah 32:2; God’s protection would keep the remnant safe from enemies and from the destruction he would bring on the wicked (Isaiah 33:14-16).

The one I love refers to the Lord; the prophet was singing this song on the Lord’s behalf. • At first, the song sounds like a love song, but by Isaiah 5:3 readers realize it is actually a complaint. • On Israel as God’s vineyard, see also Isaiah 3:14; Matthew 21:33-46; John 15:1-17.

The Song of the Vineyard expresses in poetic form God’s indictment of the wicked leadership that had ruined his vineyard, Israel. Like some wisdom literature, it presents readers with an account of a puzzling situation (Isaiah 5:1-2) before giving its spiritual significance (Isaiah 5:3-7). The theme of the vineyard’s transformation is found again in ch Isaiah 27:1-13 and in Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1).

The prophet pronounced judgment through song (Isaiah 5:1-7) and prophecies of woe (Isaiah 5:8-30). Although Israel’s future condition would be one of purity and fellowship with God (Isaiah 4:2-6), that future cannot ignore the present sinful condition of the people and their leaders.

The Lord gave the best care to his vineyard, preparing and nursing it as an expert agriculturalist. He watched over it with great attentiveness, planting the best vines—ones that had the potential for abundant sweet grapes. God had great expectations of Israel as his people (see Exodus 19:5-6), so the bitter grapes they produced—their unrighteous deeds—were useless and disappointing (cp. Galatians 5:22-23).

Clearly, the Lord had graciously done everything possible for the vineyard. He was not to blame for the bitter grapes. • you judge: Isaiah wanted the audience to condemn the vineyard before he revealed that in fact they were the vineyard (Isaiah 5:7). This rhetorical tactic is similar to the one Nathan used to confront David (2 Sam 12:1-5).

The Lord promised to make his vineyard, Israel, a desolate place because it was fit only for destruction. Later, Isaiah prophesied the gracious, glorious transformation of Israel from desolation to fruitful vitality (see Isaiah 55:13).
The withholding of rain was at times a divine judgment (Deuteronomy 28:23-24; Haggai 1:11; Haggai 2:16). It was especially devastating to a society that depended heavily on agriculture.

The identification of Israel as the vineyard is a surprise that resolves the riddle of this passage. • Here, a powerful play on Hebrew words indicted Israel. The Lord expected justice (Hebrew mishpat) but saw only oppression (mispakh) of the needy. Instead of righteousness (tsedaqah), there were cries of violence (tse‘aqah) against the poor (see Isaiah 1:21-23).

What sorrow: The first threat of judgment was against oppressive greed. Properties (house and field) were being taken by illegal means. The new owners were thugs who used every avenue to enrich themselves at the expense of the poor (see 1 Kgs 21:1-29; Amos 2:6-7).

This section contains six pronouncements of sorrow—six threats of dreadful judgment (Isaiah 5:8, Isaiah 5:11, Isaiah 5:18, Isaiah 5:20, Isaiah 5:21, Isaiah 5:22). The sorrows identify some of the “bitter grapes” produced by the vineyard of Israel (Isaiah 5:1-7).
As with drought (Isaiah 5:5-6), the reduction of crops was at times a divine judgment (see Haggai 1:6, Haggai 1:9; Haggai 2:16).
What sorrow: The second threat of judgment concerned indulgent lifestyles. The language throughout this section indicates a life of corruption.

Self-indulgent and contented, these people never think about the Lord. They were too busy enjoying their drunken parties to reflect on why things went bad in the first place, such as why God sent no rain, or why they lost a battle.

Israel and Judah would go into exile to Assyria (722 BC) and Babylon (586 BC). • The people did not respond to the Lord because they did not know him (see Isaiah 1:3). They likely knew about him, but their behavior showed that they did not know him in any intimate way.
The grave (Hebrew Sheol) represented the place of the dead in ancient Near Eastern thinking (see Isaiah 14:9).
God’s kingship is by definition just and righteous, and he will be exalted by his justice. At his exaltation, oppressors will be condemned (see Isaiah 1:21-23).
God’s ropes were “ropes of kindness and love” for Israel (Hosea 11:4).
What sorrow: The third threat of judgment was against mockers, who openly treated God’s authority with contempt.

The people challenged God to hurry up and do something to prove that he really exists and is in control of this world. The verb hurry up translates two Hebrew verbs: maher (“be quick”) and khush (“be speedy”). The same Hebrew words are used in the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz (Isaiah 8:1). • God’s plan was revealed to Isaiah. Little did the people know that God’s purposes would turn against them.
What sorrow: The fourth threat of judgment was against a lack of integrity. • evil is good . . . dark is light . . . bitter is sweet: This twisted way of looking at life corrupts God’s holy order.
What sorrow: The fifth threat of judgment concerned the folly of self-deception.
What sorrow: The sixth threat of judgment was against the indulgent lifestyle of the wicked.

The image of rotting roots reflects human transience (cp. Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 27:6; Isaiah 37:31). • To despise the Lord’s word means to ignore it, to live without regard for keeping it. Such an attitude toward God’s revelation leads to folly and ruin (Proverbs 1:30; Proverbs 5:12; Proverbs 15:5).

mountains tremble: God’s wrath against sinners is often expressed as the shaking of the earth’s foundations (Isaiah 13:13; Isaiah 23:11; Isaiah 24:18-19; Isaiah 29:6; Isaiah 54:10). God’s appearance in judgment or salvation in natural phenomena such as smoke, darkness, lightning, and earthquake is called a theophany (see Isaiah 6:1-4, Isaiah 6:6; Isaiah 13:13; Exodus 19:18-19; Psalm 18:7-15; Micah 1:3-4; Revelation 8:5; Revelation 16:17-18; Revelation 18:21-22).

The signal was a banner raised on a long pole and often placed on a high hill (see also Isaiah 13:2; Isaiah 18:3; Isaiah 30:17). The expression signal to distant nations is common in Isaiah and might be a call for participation in battle (as here) or in salvation (Isaiah 11:10, Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 49:22; Isaiah 62:10). • Distant nations refers to the Assyrians and Babylonians, who served as instruments of God’s judgment on Israel (722 BC) and on Judah (586 BC). They were the wild “animals” (Isaiah 5:5) called in to trample the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7). They would fiercely attack Israel and Judah, not letting up until God’s judgment was complete (Isaiah 5:27-30).

day of destruction (literally that day; see study note on 2:5-22). • In Old Testament prophecy, darkness represents the experience of God’s alienation, wrath, and judgment (see also Isaiah 8:22), while light stands for his holy presence (see especially Isaiah 60:2, Isaiah 60:19).

At the time of King Uzziah’s death, the Assyrians had begun to reassert their dominance in the ancient Near East. It marked the beginning of an era dominated by major world powers—Assyria, then Babylonia, Persia, Greece, and Rome. • I saw the Lord: “Lord” (Hebrew ’adonay) is used to describe human rulers as well as God. God is the supreme King. • on a lofty throne: The apostle John also had a vision of God’s heavenly throne (see Revelation 4:2; Revelation 7:10; Revelation 21:5). • If just the train of the Lord’s robe filled the Temple, how great and majestic must have been the robe itself and the one wearing it.

Isaiah’s marvelous vision of God as King on his throne served as a pivotal event in the life of the prophet. The historical circumstances surrounding this event can be interpreted in two ways: (1) Some see ch Isaiah 6:1-13 as Isaiah’s original call to ministry, meaning that chs Isaiah 1:1–5:30 and Isaiah 7:1–12:6 fit into the reign of Ahaz, who came to rule after the death of Uzziah (Isaiah 6:1). If this were so, why was Isaiah’s call not at the beginning of the book? Perhaps his call was put in ch Isaiah 6:1-13 for literary reasons, serving as a conclusion to chs Isaiah 1:1–5:30 and an introduction to chs Isaiah 7:1–12:6. The prophet’s own transformation and commissioning symbolizes the entire nation’s need for conversion if it wants to fulfill its mandate to be God’s light to the world. (2) Others understand chs Isaiah 1:1–12:6 as chronological; Isaiah’s call in ch Isaiah 6:1-13 would then serve as a recommissioning of the prophet to minister in a new way in a different period (the time of Ahaz) when his words would be rejected. Those who hold this interpretation point to Isaiah 2:7-9; Isaiah 3:16-24; Isaiah 5:8-14, contending that these passages reflect a time of prosperity, military strength, pride, and splendor; these conditions existed during Uzziah’s reign but not during Ahaz’s reign.

The mighty seraphim are heavenly beings not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture (but see also Revelation 4:6-9; Revelation 15:8). The Hebrew term might suggest an association with fire. They covered their faces so as not to look on God.

The triple usage of the word holy emphasizes the absolute separateness of the Lord. • The whole earth is filled: Because there is no verb in the Hebrew, two slightly different translations of the seraphim’s proclamation are possible. It could be that the earth, though defiled, is currently filled with his glory in creation. Or, it could mean that the earth will be filled with the glory of the Lord when he establishes his kingship on the earth in the future. Either way, the Lord’s glorious presence will one day dwell more fully on earth, despite humanity’s sinfulness and the power of wicked nations. God’s glory was further revealed in the incarnation of the Son (John 12:41; 2 Cor 3:18; 4:4-7).

It’s all over! I am doomed: The prophet felt unworthy of the vision. He was painfully aware of his personal uncleanness (sinful . . . filthy lips) when compared to the holiness of God. Isaiah knew that he was unworthy to speak the pure word of God, as were his people.

your guilt is removed, and your sins are forgiven: The prophet’s experience of forgiveness anticipated Israel’s national need for forgiveness and cleansing (Isaiah 43:25; Isaiah 44:22; see study note on 39:6-7).

Who will go for us? The Lord spoke in the presence of his angels, the heavenly council (see also 1 Kgs 22:19-22; Jeremiah 23:18, Jeremiah 23:22). • Here I am: The prophet was so overcome by the grace of God in cleansing him that he willingly committed himself to a lifetime of ministry.

do not understand . . . learn nothing: The prophet’s words brought out the heart response of his audience. The people were so sunk in sin that when they heard the truth it did not bring them closer to God but actually drove them away (e.g., Ahaz, ch Isaiah 7:1-25). Yet the truth had to be declared. Jesus also applied this principle in his own preaching (Matthew 13:14-15; Luke 8:10; Luke 19:42; John 12:40; see also Acts 28:26-27; Romans 11:8).

Isaiah was God’s agent to stimulate blindness and deafness in the wicked and sight and hearing in the godly (see also Isaiah 29:9-10, Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 42:7, Isaiah 42:16-19; Isaiah 43:8; Isaiah 56:10; Isaiah 59:10). • turn to me for healing: The Lord was ready to heal those who truly repented, but not those who merely wanted to avoid judgment while holding on to their sinful ways.
how long . . . until . . . the whole country is a wasteland: During the prophet’s ministry (740 to 685 BC), the nation was plagued by wars, famines, and other forms of devastation.

Even if a tenth—a remnant—survive, the judgment would continue until nearly all were destroyed. The prophet often spoke of near extermination or decimation (Isaiah 9:18-21; Isaiah 10:20; Isaiah 22:4; Isaiah 48:19; Isaiah 51:18) but maintained the hope of a remnant who would make a new beginning (Isaiah 7:21-22; Isaiah 29:23; Isaiah 37:31; Isaiah 44:26; Isaiah 49:19; Isaiah 54:1). • Israel’s stump will be a holy seed: The stump represents a remnant of holy people (see Isaiah 4:2-3) whose new leader would be pleasing to the Lord (Isaiah 11:1).

Rezin was king of Syria. Damascus was Syria’s capital city. • Pekah was king of Israel 740–732 BC. He was a renowned warrior (2 Chr 28:5-8). • Pekah and Rezin began to attack Jerusalem while Jotham was king (750–732 BC), and they intensified their efforts during the early years of young King Ahaz (2 Kgs 15:37; 16:5).

At one point in his reign, Ahaz found himself in a crisis. The leaders of Syria and Israel attacked Judah. They planned to replace Ahaz and force Judah to join them in their resistance against Assyria. Ahaz responded by calling Assyria in to help him (2 Kgs 16:7-10), thus refusing Isaiah’s challenge to trust the Lord instead (Isaiah 7:12). Although the Assyrians squelched the alliance of Syria and Israel, leading to the eventual downfall of both those nations, they also soon set their sights on total domination of Judah.

The historical context of these prophecies involved Assyria’s rise to power and the alliance between Syria and Israel as enemies of Judah (Isaiah 7:1-2; see 2 Kgs 16:5). Assyria became God’s rod to punish Syria, Israel, and Judah (Isa Isaiah 7:1–10:34).
In this long section of the book, the nation of Israel was confronted with a vision of God, similar to how Isaiah was confronted in ch Isaiah 6:1-13.
hearts . . . trembled with fear: In contrast, Ahaz’s son King Hezekiah faced the Assyrians some thirty years later with great faith (701 BC; see Isaiah 37:6-7, Isaiah 37:14-20).
The aqueduct was a place where political negotiations took place later during Hezekiah’s reign (see Isaiah 36:2).

he doesn’t need to fear: This was a “fear not” prophecy (common in Isaiah) in which the Lord assured his people of his presence and purpose. • two burned-out embers: If Ahaz had God’s perspective, he would have seen that Rezin and Pekah were minor threats who were about to be extinguished.
The son of Tabeel, otherwise unknown, was obviously sympathetic to Israel’s and Syria’s resistance against Assyria.

The Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal had Israel resettled with people from other places within sixty-five years (by 670 BC; see 2 Kgs 17:24-34). • Damascus was crushed and completely destroyed by 732 BC, and Samaria was crushed by 722 BC.

The last sentence is a play on two Hebrew words: If you do not have faith (ta’aminu), you will not stand firm (te’amenu). Firm trust in the Lord is utterly essential, especially for a leader of God’s people (see also 2 Chr 20:20), and it must be firmly acted upon in order to demonstrate that it exists. Ahaz and his contemporaries trusted their enemy (Assyria) rather than God. By contrast, Hezekiah later demonstrated his faith in the Lord in a similar context (see Isaiah 36:1–38:22).
A sign of confirmation would be performed before Ahaz’s eyes as a token of God’s truthfulness. His son Hezekiah would also receive such a sign (see Isaiah 37:30).

I will not test the Lord like that: Despite this seemingly pious response (based on Deuteronomy 6:16), Ahaz was most likely already in negotiations with the Assyrians and had already decided whom he would trust for rescue in this war.

This prophecy received its ultimate fulfillment in the birth of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:18-24). Yet it is likely that it also had a partial fulfillment in Isaiah’s day, either with the birth of godly king Hezekiah, Ahaz’s son, or with the birth of one of Isaiah’s children. The similar sequence of the verbs in Isaiah 7:14 and Isaiah 8:3 (conceive . . . give birth . . . call) and the link between Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz in Isaiah 8:5-10 suggest that Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz were the same person. • The name Immanuel (which means ‘God is with us’) symbolized God’s presence and protection. God was with Judah during the attack by the alliance of Syria and Israel (734 BC), in the Assyrian crisis (701 BC), and throughout their prolonged existence until their fall in 586 BC. The kingdom of Israel fell during the time of Isaiah (722 BC). The assurance “I am with you” remained significant even in the exilic and postexilic periods (Isaiah 41:10; Isaiah 43:2, Isaiah 43:5). The greatest assurance ultimately came in Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God (Matthew 1:23; see also Revelation 12:5).

By the time this child is old enough: The crisis involving the alliance of Syria and Israel against Judah was in 734 BC; by 732 BC Damascus, capital of Syria, was destroyed, and the northern kingdom, Israel, was defeated. • choose what is right and reject what is wrong: This was to happen by the age of 12, when a child was held responsible as an adult. In 722 BC, Israel went into exile. • he will be eating yogurt and honey: The land would be so depopulated that these delicacies would be available to all.

Israel broke away from Judah in 931 BC (see 1 Kgs 12:19-20). • will bring the king of Assyria upon you: Ahaz called Assyria in to help (2 Kgs 16:8-9), but Assyria turned against him and made Judah a vassal state.

The repetition of in that day referred to the yet future day of the Lord. Judah would experience the judgment already announced by Isaiah as a foretaste of an even greater judgment to come: exile in Babylon (586–538 BC).
Locations such as desolate valleys, caves, and thorny places were places of refuge for the desperate (see Isaiah 2:10). However, Judah’s enemies would find them there.

shave off everything: your land, your crops, and your people: In the ancient Near East, forced shaving was an act of disgrace (see 2 Sam 10:4-5). Here it was a metaphor for the despoiling of the country.
Farmers faced near total disaster. Fertile agricultural fields (lush vineyards) would revert to wild grazing lands dominated by worthless plants (briers and thorns; see Isaiah 5:6).

The meaning of the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz (“Swift to plunder and quick to carry away”) applies both to Judah’s enemies (Isaiah 8:4) and to Judah itself (Isaiah 8:7-8). They had trusted Assyria in place of God, and now Assyria would turn on them and all but destroy them. God was with them (Immanuel; see Isaiah 7:14), but his presence would be destructive if they refused to trust in him (see Isaiah 8:14).

my wife: Literally the prophetess. • Like the name Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14), Maher-shalal-hash-baz is symbolic. It is possible that this child was the partial fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy as well (see study note on 7:14). The ultimate fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy occurred with the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:22-23).
before this child is old enough: See also Isaiah 7:16. • Damascus and Samaria were ruined and destroyed in 732 BC, fulfilling this verse along with Isaiah 7:8, Isaiah 7:19-20.
This prophecy connects the sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz with the sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 8:8, Isaiah 8:10).

The gently flowing waters of Shiloah supplied Jerusalem with water. Here they represent God’s loving presence and provision (see Psalm 46:4). • Ahaz rejected the sign and the promise of God’s protection. He was not a man of faith (Isaiah 7:9), and now the people were following in his footsteps by placing their hope in Assyria to save them from King Rezin and King Pekah (cp. Isaiah 7:7-9, Isaiah 7:16).

The mighty flood from the Euphrates River represents the invading Assyrian army (see Jeremiah 47:2). The river would overflow all its channels when the Assyrians marched deep into Judah. This stood as a frightening contrast with the gently flowing waters of Shiloah (Isaiah 8:6).

chin deep: Judah barely survived the Assyrian assaults in 701 BC (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38). • submerging your land from one end to the other: From north to south, Judah was nearly devastated, except for the city of Jerusalem (see Isaiah 1:8-9; chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38). • Immanuel: Despite their failure to trust him and the disaster it brought, God was still with his people (see Isaiah 7:14).
God’s plan to rescue his stubborn people would ultimately be fulfilled. God planned to destroy Assyria, just as he does every other proud nation that rejects him or boasts in its own power.
God is with us: See Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8.

This text reveals the heart of Isaiah’s message. The issue was fear of the Lord versus fear of people (see Isaiah 7:9; Isaiah 8:6). When an individual fears people, the Lord becomes a trap and destruction is certain (cp. Proverbs 29:25; see “Fearing People” Theme Note). For those who fear the Lord, he becomes a sanctuary; their salvation is assured.

People regarded Isaiah’s message of non-involvement with Assyria as treasonous, part of a conspiracy. But Isaiah was not trying to play political games; rather, he proclaimed God’s message. • What frightens them was the alliance of Syria and Israel attacking Judah (see Isaiah 7:1, Isaiah 7:4).

To make the Lord . . . holy meant giving him first place in life and acknowledging that nothing is greater than he is. • Fear of God means reverencing him as God (Proverbs 1:7). The people of Judah were not to fear Israel and Syria or the Assyrians (Isaiah 7:9; Isaiah 10:24).

He will keep you safe (literally he will be a sanctuary): God is a place of refuge. • stone . . . stumble . . . rock . . . fall: By trusting Assyria rather than God, the people of Jerusalem would find themselves in a trap and a snare as the Assyrians turned against them. For those who trust in the Lord, however, he is faithful and strong (Isaiah 28:16; see Psalm 118:22-23; Luke 2:34; Romans 9:32-33; 1 Pet 2:6-8).
instructions (Hebrew torah): The Torah defined Israel’s covenant relationship with God, but the people were quick to forget (see also Isaiah 1:10).

The command to preserve Isaiah’s teaching suggests that it was harshly received by his contemporaries, who might have wanted to snuff it out. Faithful disciples safely preserved the prophet’s messages.

I will wait for the Lord . . . I will put my hope in him: Isaiah’s message against Syria, Israel, and Assyria would be proven true in the historical events that followed. The fulfillment would further encourage the godly to await the final downfall of all ungodly power structures (see Isaiah 8:9-10). Waiting for the Lord requires submission, prayer, hope, and faith (see Isaiah 25:9; Isaiah 26:8; Isaiah 33:2), resulting in a quiet spirit and a renewal of inner strength (Isaiah 40:31). The book of Hebrews applies these words to Jesus Christ (Hebrews 2:13). • God had turned away; the people of Israel and Judah were alienated from the Lord because of their sin.

I and the children the Lord has given me (see the application to Jesus Christ in Hebrews 2:13): The names of the prophet Isaiah and his children carried significance as signs and warnings. Shear-jashub (a remnant will return; Isaiah 7:3) was a sign of God’s faithfulness to Judah. Maher-shalal-hash-baz (swift to plunder and quick to carry away) signified the destruction of Damascus and Samaria (Isaiah 8:1-4) and the desolation of faithless Judah (Isaiah 8:5-8). The name of Isaiah (Yahweh is salvation) itself signifies that salvation is from the Lord alone. These three names also represent major themes in the book: the remnant, the desolation of Judah, and salvation. Immanuel (God is with us) embodies all of these themes, along with the idea that Judah would be protected if only it would trust in the Lord.

Isaiah contrasts his counsel with that of his ungodly contemporaries. Isaiah’s message gives light, whereas the message of the spiritists led to darkness and death. • Mediums used various means of divination, including summoning the dead, in the attempt to determine the future (see Isaiah 19:3). God had banned these useless activities (Isaiah 47:9; Deuteronomy 18:9-11).
God gave instructions and teachings through the law and through his prophets, such as Isaiah (see Isaiah 8:16).

Zebulun and Naphtali were northern tribes in Israel (Judges 6:35). They were humbled by the Assyrian invaders under Tiglath-pileser III in 734 and 732 BC. In Jesus’ lifetime, this prophecy was connected with his coming out of Galilee (Matthew 4:14-16). • Galilee of the Gentiles was the region of Israel between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea. It was heavily influenced—culturally, religiously, and politically—by the surrounding Gentile nations.

Beyond destruction there is hope. In the Messiah’s kingdom, the darkness would give way to great light, which was to dawn in Galilee and reach the whole nation, and then the whole world. The Messiah’s rule would be marked by the vindication of the oppressed and the end of all oppression. He would bring justice and righteousness forever in a kingdom of peace.

The people experienced the rule of other nations as a yoke of . . . slavery and a heavy burden (Jeremiah 30:8). • oppressor’s rod: In Isaiah 10:5, the Assyrians are called “the rod of [the Lord’s] anger.” Just as God’s anger will cease, so will Assyria’s oppression of Judah (Isaiah 14:5). • The Lord had destroyed the army of Midian through Gideon (see Judges 6:35; Judges 7:22-25).
Burning the boots and uniforms marked the end of the need for instruments of war.

a child is born to us, a son is given to us: This child, the Messiah, would be David’s descendant (Isaiah 11:1). • he will be called: These names can be read as four throne names, signifying the nature of the child’s rule: (1) The Wonderful Counselor conforms to God’s wisdom (Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 25:1; Isaiah 28:29; Isaiah 40:13), unlike the counselors of Judah (Isaiah 1:26; Isaiah 3:3). (2) Mighty God is an affirmation of the Messiah’s divine nature. (3) He cares for his children as the Everlasting Father, the father whose care continues forever (cp. Isaiah 22:21; Isaiah 63:16). (4) The Prince of Peace is a leader who brings peace. • Alternatively, the four names could be collapsed into two: (1) “A Wonderful Counselor [is] the Mighty God”; and (2) “the Everlasting Father [is] a Prince of Peace” (on his nature, see Isaiah 11:1-9). • Jesus Christ, the Son of David (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32; see also Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:3, Isaiah 8:18), will bring in the kingdom of his peace (Revelation 19:1-21).

Like Ahaz, this ruler will be a descendant of David. Unlike Ahaz and the rulers of Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:21-23), he would trust God and rule with justice and righteousness (Isaiah 11:1-3). Jesus the Messiah reigns for all eternity (Luke 1:32-33).

This prophecy of judgment was against the northern kingdom of Israel. Despite God’s message that the Assyrians would crush them (chs Isaiah 7:1–8:22), the people of Samaria were foolishly confident that they could withstand the siege.
In their proud confidence, Israel thought it would replace whatever was lost with more expensive items (see Isaiah 2:13-16; Amos 5:11).
Rezin’s enemies were the Assyrians (Isaiah 7:4, Isaiah 7:17; Isaiah 8:4). Rezin was king of Syria (see ch Isaiah 7:1-25).
God’s punishment was intended to bring repentance, not destruction; but Israel was apostate and refused to repent or seek the Lord.
Even widows and orphans, ordinarily objects of God’s compassion (Isaiah 1:17, Isaiah 1:23; Isaiah 10:2), became objects of his wrath when they were unrepentant.
Following the decimation of leadership, civil war would destroy the nation like an out-of-control brushfire.

Manasseh and Ephraim represent the northern kingdom as its largest tribes. The two largest tribes of Israel and Judah fought amongst themselves. This is probably a reference to the war between Judah and the alliance of Syria and Israel, which is commonly called the Syro-Ephraimite War (Isaiah 7:1-12). In that conflict, brothers savagely fought against brothers (2 Chr 28).
What sorrow introduces a threat of divine judgment.
This prophecy was directed against Judah’s leaders, who used their positions to enrich themselves at the people’s expense.
The implied answer to Isaiah’s rhetorical questions was that there would be no one to turn to when God punished Judah. • Disaster came first from the distant land of Assyria and later from Babylon.
The Assyrians were God’s instrument (rod . . . club) in judging Syria, Israel, and Judah, but they would not go unpunished for their own wickedness.

This judgment was pronounced on Assyria because of their ruthless destruction of nations (Isaiah 10:7), blasphemous boasting (Isaiah 10:12), oppression (Isaiah 10:13-14), and self-perceived autonomy (Isaiah 10:15).

The primacy of the Lord’s moral law was established in Isaiah 9:8–10:4; this passage works out the implications of the law: (1) Assyria was only a tool in God’s hands and was therefore as liable to judgment by God as any other nation (Isaiah 10:5-19, Isaiah 10:28-34); (2) those among God’s people who trusted in him and obeyed his covenant would be rescued (Isaiah 10:20-27); and (3) God would establish his kingdom on earth (ch Isaiah 11:1-16).

Despite their privileged calling as God’s covenant people, Judah had become a godless nation, making them the object of God’s anger (Isaiah 10:4). • The word plunder translates both the Hebrew words shalal and baz, recalling the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz (see Isaiah 5:19; Isaiah 8:1, Isaiah 8:3, Isaiah 8:5-10).

will not understand: The Assyrians did not realize they were following God’s intended purpose to punish Israel and Judah. Because they went about savagely killing and looting other nations of their own accord, God would also hold them guilty.

We destroyed: By 717 BC, the regions to the north of Judah were firmly in Assyrian hands. Calno, in northern Syria (referred to as Calneh in Amos 6:2), fell to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC. Carchemish, on the Euphrates River, was taken by King Sargon II in 717 BC. Hamath, on the Orontes River, was subjugated in 738 and 720 BC. Arpad was located south of Calno. Damascus and Samaria, the capitals of Syria and Israel, were taken in 732 and 722 BC, respectively (Isaiah 7:8; Isaiah 8:4).
whose gods were greater than those in Jerusalem and Samaria: Assyria would make this argument while threatening Jerusalem (Isaiah 36:19-20; Isaiah 37:12).

Assyria destroyed Samaria under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II in 722 BC (2 Kgs 17:3-6). If Samaria and Judah worshiped the same God, and Assyria had already defeated Samaria, the king of Assyria could expect to defeat Judah also.
Any royal power that exalts itself against the Lord, the Great King, is proud and arrogant (see Isaiah 2:11-12) and will be crushed.

my own powerful arm . . . my own shrewd wisdom (cp. Isaiah 10:5): God alone is all-powerful and wise. He plans the future, and he determines which nations will rise to power and which will be defeated.

ax . . . saw . . . rod . . . wooden cane: Such instruments are only as good as the person who uses them. Assyria considered itself independent of the hand of God, but their conquests were made possible only by his permission and to serve his purposes (Isaiah 10:5).
The fulfillment of this prophecy was in 701 BC, when 185,000 Assyrian troops were killed by plague and flaming fire (see Isaiah 37:36).

left . . . the survivors: A remnant from Jerusalem barely survived, but their safety was secure because God promised to preserve them (see Isaiah 1:8-9; Isaiah 4:2; Isaiah 6:13; Isaiah 37:31-32). • All these wars would teach the Israelite remnant to no longer depend on allies such as Assyria. Instead, they would faithfully trust in the Lord (see Isaiah 8:13; Isaiah 17:7).
In the midst of Assyrian oppression, there was hope for the remnant. This passage develops more fully the meaning of Shear-jashub, a remnant will return (Isaiah 10:21; see Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 8:18).

God had similarly promised descendants as numerous as the sand of the seashore to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). • rightly decided to destroy: God’s decision was a just response to the people’s persistent wickedness.
as the Egyptians did long ago: See Exodus 1:8–2:25.
God assured his people of his presence and purpose.
Gideon triumphed over the Midianites: See Judges 7:25.
Israel’s bondage ended in 539 BC with a new exodus from exile.

Look, the Assyrians are now at Aiath: The march described in Isaiah 10:29-32 is a poetic account of Assyria’s defeat. The places follow a route from the north down to Jerusalem. Upon arriving at Jerusalem, the Assyrians were forced to retreat. God was with Jerusalem, and eventually Assyria would be utterly destroyed. This passage might foretell Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38), but it could just as well describe an earlier or later invasion.

stump . . . shoot . . . new Branch . . . from the old root: This new growth refers to the continuity of David’s royal family line despite its virtual cessation during the Exile (see also Isaiah 6:13; Isaiah 39:7; Revelation 22:16). The new growth from the old roots would not be like the former frail and unjust descendants of David (see Isaiah 4:2). Jesus, the Messiah, is the final fulfillment.

The kingdom of the Messiah, first introduced in Isaiah 9:1-7, is now considered in more detail. Isaiah challenged the Israelites about why they would trust in any of the nations when God had far better plans in mind.

The Spirit of the Lord will rest on the Messiah. The succession of David’s line is guaranteed by the Spirit. The Messiah’s coming would bring justice and righteousness (Isaiah 11:4), peace (Isaiah 11:8), and the extension of the Kingdom to the nations (Isaiah 11:10; see also Isaiah 32:15-16). • The promised Messiah would have great wisdom and understanding, like Solomon, as well as knowledge and the fear of the Lord (1 Kgs 3:28; 4:29; Proverbs 1:1-7; Proverbs 2:6-7). • The Spirit of counsel and might alludes to Isaiah 9:6. The Messiah will be full of wisdom and will have the power to execute his righteous rule.
obeying the Lord: Literally the fear of the Lord, as in Isaiah 11:2 (see Proverbs 1:7).

The poor and . . . the exploited would receive the justice due to them, which the wicked leaders of Judah had previously withheld. • the force of his word: Literally the scepter of his mouth (see Psalm 2:9; Revelation 19:15).
By virtue of the righteous character of the Messiah, his reign will be characterized by justice, righteousness, and truth, in contrast to the conditions of Jerusalem described in Isaiah 1:21.

In that day means in the coming age of the Messiah. The prophecy that follows received partial fulfillment in Isaiah’s day or shortly thereafter. The final fulfillment is found in the coming of the Messiah to inaugurate and then fully establish the age to come.
Nothing will hurt or destroy: There will be no evildoers, corruption, or sin on God’s holy mountain (Zion).

the heir to David’s throne: Literally the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1; Revelation 5:5; Revelation 22:16). • The Messiah will bring salvation to all the world (Isaiah 2:1-5). Members of other nations will even serve as priests and Levites (Isaiah 66:20-21), but only if they repent and believe in the true God.

The first time the Lord reached out his hand was at the Exodus; the second time will occur in the future when the Messiah gathers Gentiles (Isaiah 11:10) and his own people who live among the Gentile nations (Isaiah 11:11). The Exodus remained the paradigm of hope for those in exile (see Isaiah 11:16; Isaiah 35:8; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 43:19-20; Isaiah 48:21). • The remnant of his people included Israelites who survived the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions and were sent into exile.

jealousy between Israel and Judah: The two kingdoms had become enemies during Judah’s war with the alliance of Syria and Israel (see Isaiah 7:1-12). In the future, they would cooperate in joint military expeditions.
Philistia to the west: The Philistines were Israel’s historic enemy. • The nations to the east included the Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites. All foes would be vanquished.

Using imagery from Israel’s past exodus, Isaiah encouraged his listeners by promising that God would bring his people out of Assyria the way he brought them out of Egypt (Exodus 14:29–15:18; see also Revelation 16:12).
God’s comfort is the main subject of chs Isaiah 40:1–66:24.

The prophet’s personal song of praise for God’s salvation closes the meditations on trust in chs Isaiah 7:1–12:6. God will prove himself trustworthy in his promises to rescue his people even though they initially refused to trust him. The song anticipates chs Isaiah 40:1–66:24 with its themes of salvation, forgiveness, praise, joy, and the nations.

God’s promise to save includes reconciliation (Isaiah 1:18), participation (Isaiah 11:10), cleansing and protection (Isaiah 4:3-6), peace and confidence (Isaiah 32:16-17), and restoration (Isaiah 11:6-9). • Lord God (Hebrew Yah Yahweh): The first word is an abbreviation of the second. • The Lord God is my strength and my song: See Exodus 15:2; Psalm 118:14.
God’s salvation is like a deep and unending source of water that provides life (see also Isaiah 41:18; Psalm 87:7).
Tell the nations what he has done: The story of salvation must be told, even beyond the community of Israel (Psalm 67:2; Psalm 70:4; Psalm 98:2).
See Psalm 48:1; Psalm 96:4; Psalm 99:2.

At the time of this prophecy, Assyria was the major power. Isaiah anticipated the rise of Babylon as an even crueler kingdom that would destroy Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 39:6-7; chs Isaiah 46:1–47:15). The universal language of Isaiah 13:1–14:23 suggests that in this context, Babylon represents all wicked and arrogant nations in the same way that “Babylon the Great” does in the book of Revelation (Revelation 18:1-24). Therefore, while this description of Babylon’s fall applies to the fall of historic Babylon in 539 BC, it also applies until the final judgment against the ultimate kingdom of evil (Revelation 19:1-21).

This section contains prophecies of judgment against the nations. By including a prophecy against Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 22:1-25) in the midst of prophecies against the pagan nations, Isaiah emphasized that Israel’s identity as God’s people would not protect them from God’s punishment when they sinned as the other nations do.

A signal flag or banner that could be seen clearly from a great distance was often placed on a bare hilltop as a call to battle. • God stands against Babylon as the symbolic representative of all evil kingdoms.

Just as Assyria was the rod of his anger (Isaiah 9:4; Isaiah 10:5, Isaiah 10:15), other nations serve as the Lord’s weapons and carry out his will. The Medes and Persians conquered Babylon in 539 BC. • God’s wrath is an expression of his justice as well as his intent to restore order to the world by obliterating evildoers (Isaiah 10:25-26; see Lamentations 2:22; Ezekiel 7:19).

When pronouncing judgment that is still in the future, the prophets sometimes spoke as though it had already arrived. This emphasized the urgency of turning back to God (Ezekiel 30:3; Joel 1:15; Joel 3:14; Obadiah 1:15; Zephaniah 1:7).
Pangs . . . like those of a woman in labor: The day of the Lord brings sudden and overpowering pain and fear for the wicked (see also Jeremiah 30:6; Hosea 13:13; Micah 4:9, Micah 4:10; Micah 5:3).

Cosmic upheaval and darkness are common images for the day of the Lord, a time of God’s judgment (see also Ezekiel 32:7-8; Joel 2:10, Joel 2:31; Joel 3:15; Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24; Revelation 6:12-13; Revelation 8:12; cp. Isaiah 30:26).
punish the world: See Revelation 20:11.
Solomon’s imported gold came from Ophir (1 Kgs 9:28).

God will shake the heavens. The earth will move: Cosmic upheaval will accompany God’s coming in judgment (see study note on 5:25; see also Haggai 2:7, Haggai 2:21; Hebrews 12:26-27; Revelation 16:17-18; Revelation 18:21-22).
These terrible acts of war would be perpetrated against Babylon, itself a cruel conquering power (see also Psalm 137:8-9; Jeremiah 6:11-12; Nahum 3:10).
The Lord is sovereign and controls history. He can stir up kingdoms to execute his will. • The Medes from northwestern Iran joined Persian King Cyrus in fighting against Babylon in 539 BC.
This picture of Babylon as a perpetually haunted ruin contrasts with its magnificence at its peak (see Daniel 4:29-30).

Babylon will never be inhabited again: Babylon, often a symbol of idolatry, immorality, imperialism, and oppression in Scripture, will one day come completely to an end (see Revelation 18:2; Revelation 19:2).

The Hebrew word here translated mercy draws from the imagery of a woman’s maternal care for her child to illustrate God’s merciful love for his people (see also Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:13). • God had initially chosen Israel as his special people when he called Abraham (see Isaiah 41:8; Genesis 12:1-3). Although their status did not change during the Exile, they faced God’s wrath like any other wicked nation because they had rejected him. • settle once again in their own land: This promise began to be fulfilled in 538 BC (see Ezra 1:1-11). • People from many different nations would join Israel as the people of God (see also Isaiah 2:3-4; Isaiah 11:11-12; Isaiah 19:18-25; Isaiah 60:1-14).
This message for Israel separates two prophecies of judgment against Babylon (ch Isaiah 13:1-22; Isaiah 14:3-23).

Just as Israel was subject to the Lord, so the nations of the world would submit themselves to the Lord through Israel (Isaiah 45:14; Isaiah 49:7, Isaiah 49:23; Isaiah 60:12, Isaiah 60:14; Isaiah 66:23). • The oppressed nation of Israel will rule over its enemies, assuming a position of power and favor with God.
God gives . . . rest (i.e., relief; Isaiah 28:12; see Deuteronomy 25:19; 2 Sam 7:11) from the sorrow and fear, . . . slavery and chains Israel experienced under foreign oppressors (see Isaiah 9:4).
This taunting song for the king of Babylon is in the form of a funeral dirge (cp. Revelation 18:1-24).
A taunt is a mocking comparison in song form. In this instance, the king of Babylon is compared to a dead man entering the world of the dead.

The land and people will be at rest and quiet because the oppression has ended and the king of Babylon has died. • The whole creation will join in praise, able to sing again (see also Isaiah 42:11; Isaiah 44:23; cp. Romans 8:22).

The Babylonians saw the place of the dead (Hebrew Sheol) as a place of no return. • stand up (literally get up from their thrones): The thrones reflect the Babylonian concept of the life hereafter as a continuation of the same mode of existence as the present life. It appears that the other kings are honoring the great king of Babylon, but the next verses tell a different story.
weak as we are: The Babylonian king had no power over anyone after death and was unable to leave Sheol. The Israelites will mock this great king who on earth appeared to have no weaknesses.
Babylon’s might and power and the sound of the harp were ended, and its magnificence was destroyed (see also Revelation 18:22). • Maggots and worms symbolized death and decomposition (Isaiah 66:24).

fallen from heaven, O shining star: These words allude to the Canaanite story of the god Helel’s rebellion against the god El (chief deity of the Canaanite pantheon) and his fall from heaven. Some see the fall of the king of Babylon here as symbolizing the fall of Satan (see Ezekiel 28:1-26; Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:9). However, there is little to suggest that Isaiah understood it in that way. He was thinking of the historical king of Babylon. • son of the morning: The battle took place under the early morning sun. The Latin Vulgate translates the term as Lucifer (morning star), a name for Satan in Christian tradition, but the Hebrew text makes no apparent reference here to Satan.

This verse alludes to the Canaanite belief that the chief god El and the other gods were enthroned on Mount Zaphon, a northern mountain (see Psalm 48:2; for a New Testament application, see Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15).
Most High: See Genesis 14:19-22.

This is a restatement of Isaiah 14:9-11. The dead spirits inhabiting the place of the dead will be startled and amazed that the Babylonian king, who ruled the world with his merciless might, has absolutely no power in death.
The absence of a proper burial was a sign of great shame and dishonor. Unlike other kings, the king of Babylon would be disgraced in judgment.

As another sign of disgrace, the king of Babylon would have no children to provide a future legacy. • because of their father’s sins: God looks at individuals in relationship to their families and their people. Here, the Babylonian king’s children had joint responsibility for their father’s actions (see also Deuteronomy 5:9-10).
Isaiah summarized the previous taunt (Isaiah 14:3-21) with this prophecy, spoken in the first person. God decrees the destruction and desolation of Babylon.

I have planned . . . I have decided: No nation can either diminish or resist God’s plans to bring judgment against Assyria or his plans in general. The prophets understood and communicated God’s plan so that his people could respond appropriately.
This prophecy resumes declaring judgment on Assyria (see ch Isaiah 10:1-34). The placement of this prophecy after the judgment against Babylon suggests close connections between Assyria and Babylon.
This prophecy told what would happen when Sennacherib attacked Hezekiah some years later in 701 BC (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38).
The Lord’s power over Assyria is just one example of his sovereignty over the whole earth.

The king who attacked Philistia was probably Ahaz (Isaiah 14:28). • a more poisonous snake: This probably refers to one of the later Assyrian kings, either Sennacherib (701 BC), Esarhaddon (680 BC), or Ashurbanipal (668 BC).
The advancing army, probably Assyria, would stir up clouds of dust like smoke that were ominously visible in the north.

The Lord has built Jerusalem: God was fully willing and capable of defending Judah, and he did not want the kingdom to make alliances with nations such as the Philistines to protect themselves from the invading Assyrians.
Moab was Judah’s enemy, situated on the eastern side of the Dead Sea. • In one night: Destruction would be sudden and decisive.
This message of judgment and lament concerned Moab’s fall. The extensive references to Moabite place names indicate that Isaiah was thoroughly familiar with Moab.
In the ancient Near East, actions such as shaving or cutting off their beards revealed deep sorrow (see Jeremiah 48:37).
Heshbon was the former capital of Sihon (Numbers 21:23-26). • Elealeh was located close to Heshbon. • Jahaz was between Heshbon and the Arnon River (see Jeremiah 48:34).
My heart weeps for Moab: The prophet joined in the lament to express the greatness of Moab’s pain. • Zoar was in the southeastern area of the Dead Sea (Genesis 14:2; Genesis 19:23).

Identification of the waters of Nimrim is uncertain (see also Jeremiah 48:34). • dried up . . . scorched . . . tender plants: For the theme of natural resources drying up as a form of judgment, see study note on Isa 24:4.
The precise locations of the Ravine of Willows and of Eglaim and Beer-elim are uncertain.
Dibon: The Masoretic Text reads Dimon, which is a play on the word translated blood (Hebrew dam). • blood: Apparently many people from Moab had already been killed, but their judgment had only begun.

Moab was known for its sheep (see 2 Kgs 3:4). The lambs were sent as tribute to Judah in recognition of Judah’s sovereignty over Moab. • Sela (the cliff), an unknown remote site, was apparently where the Moabites escaped through the desert.
A request for asylum.
Do not betray us . . . Hide them: Moab’s situation would become so dire that they would beg for asylum in other lands.
This prophecy of salvation spoke of the future of David’s dynasty. • Activities such as oppression and destruction would cease with the end of Moabite hostilities (see 2 Kgs 13:20).
God would establish one of David’s descendants as king (see also Isaiah 9:7; Isaiah 11:1-5, Isaiah 11:10-12).
The Moabites’ hardened state of pride and arrogance and rage and boasting prevented them from humbling themselves before God.
The response to Moab’s request for asylum (Isaiah 16:1-4).

The vineyards at Sibmah were located by the Moabite city of Heshbon. • Moab was like a luxuriant vine that extends far and wide, but Israel’s beautiful vine reached to the ends of the earth (Isaiah 27:6). • The location of Jazer is unknown.
The hilltops were sites for pagan shrines (see Isaiah 15:2). • No one will be able to save them, including the idols the Moabites called on for protection (see Isaiah 40:18-19; Isaiah 44:18-19).

Within three years, counting each day (literally Within three years, as a servant bound by contract would count them; see also Isaiah 21:16): A man who had sold himself into servitude for a period of time would calculate how much time remained right down to the final day. This verse refers to events that are unknown. • The glory of Moab will be ended, probably because of the Assyrian conquest of Moab (late 700s BC). • only a feeble few will be left alive: Though decimated by war, the Moabites still existed during Nehemiah’s time (Nehemiah 13:23).
Damascus, the ringleader in the alliance of Syria and Israel against Judah, fell when the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III invaded in 732 BC.

This section contains prophecies of judgment against Damascus, Israel, Ethiopia, and Egypt. The scene moves from the crisis of 734 BC (the alliance of Syria and Israel—see study note on 7:1-25) to the Assyrian crisis in 701 BC (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38).
The towns of Aroer were east of the Dead Sea (see 2 Kgs 10:32-33). • Flocks will graze in the streets: The city would be useless for any other purpose.
The strategic fortified towns of Israel were the pride of Israel, but they could not resist God’s purposes.
Israel’s glory will grow dim: God will judge all human pride. • Israel’s robust body will waste away like a person who is ill.
The vision shifts from Damascus (Isaiah 17:1-3) to the northern kingdom of Israel; Damascus and Israel were allies in the war against Judah, and both were later destroyed by Assyria.
The valley of Rephaim was a fertile valley in Judah; however, it looked bare after each harvest.
Although the God of Israel judged the wickedness of Israel, he was still its God.
The people referred to here are either Israelites or humanity at large. • look . . . turn their eyes: They will again put their trust in the Lord.
Canaanites and then Israelites worshiped the fertility goddess Asherah in wooded areas or, in the absence of wooded areas, using Asherah poles (see Isaiah 27:9; Isaiah 65:3; Micah 5:14).
The Hivites and Amorites were members of the original population of Canaan; they were to be destroyed when the Israelites conquered the land (see Deuteronomy 20:17).

The Israelites had mixed faith in the Lord with elements of Baal worship. They turned from the Lord, who alone is God and will not be held alongside an idol in people’s hearts. • The term Rock refers to the Lord’s ability to provide refuge (see Isaiah 26:4; Isaiah 30:29; Psalm 18:2, Psalm 18:46).
At times, the sea represents opposition to God (see Job 7:12; Job 26:12; Psalm 46:3; Psalm 93:3).
God was present with Judah during the crisis.
God will silence them: The Lord is sovereign over the nations, as he is over the sea (Psalm 65:7).
In the evening . . . by dawn: Despite frightening circumstances, Israel can have confidence in the Lord’s ability to save quickly (see Isaiah 37:36-38).
Ethiopia was at the southern extremity of the kingdom of Egypt. At the time, Egypt was ruled by the dynasty of the Ethiopian Piankhi.
Both the battle flag and ram’s horn were used to marshal and send signals to armies in battle (see Judges 3:27; Judges 6:34; 2 Sam 2:28).
The Lord is untroubled by human activities; he watches quietly from his dwelling place and acts in his own time (see Psalm 2:1-4).
your plans are ripening: Ethiopia had made every effort to form alliances to protect itself against Assyria, but its alliance with Judah would not help.

Conquered or weaker nations were often forced to pay tribute to a dominant king in the region (see Isaiah 16:1; 2 Kgs 3:4-5). The Ethiopians would come bringing gifts to honor the Lord for his defeat of the Assyrians (see also 2 Chr 32:23).

Riding on a swift cloud shows God’s sovereignty and power over creation (Psalm 104:3). He is coming in judgment against Judah’s enemies (see Deuteronomy 33:26; Psalm 18:9-10; Psalm 68:4; Psalm 97:2-3). • The idols of Egypt tremble because they are weak and impotent, unable to help (see Isaiah 40:18; Isaiah 45:16; Isaiah 46:1).
Egypt was vulnerable, depending on the Nile for food, fish, and industry. When the Lord struck the Nile, Egypt would be in dire straits, and their gods would not be able to help.
See also Jeremiah 46:1-28; Ezekiel 29:1–32:32.
Egypt had a history of civil wars that ravaged the country. Egypt’s fragile unity was breaking apart.
Idols . . . spirits, mediums, and those who consult the spirits of the dead were called upon in an attempt to ward off impending destruction (see Isaiah 8:19-22; Isaiah 47:12-13).
hard, cruel master: In 671 BC, the Assyrian king Esarhaddon invaded Egypt and destroyed the royal city of Memphis. In 663 BC, Ashurbanipal attacked and destroyed Thebes (see Nahum 3:8-10).

The waters of the Nile were Egypt’s lifeline. Any disturbance in the regular pattern of flooding affected the whole nation. In ancient Egypt, the Nile was considered to be a god. However, the true God could easily dry it up.
There was no flax or thread: The drought crippled the linen industry.

Zoan was the capital of Egypt, located in the Nile delta (see Numbers 13:22). • officials . . . best counsel: The king depended on the strategies and counsel of wise men (Isaiah 19:12; see Genesis 41:39-40). • The officials of Zoan were known for all their wise ancestors, and Egypt liked to brag about them.
The prophet taunted the leaders and wise men of Egypt, who were helpless to avert tragedy.
Where are your wise counselors: Cp. 1 Cor 1:20.
Memphis was an ancient capital in Egypt located south of the Nile delta. It was destroyed by Esarhaddon in 671 BC.

There is nothing Egypt can do: No leader, idol, or conventional wisdom can stand against God’s judgment. • The head and the tail represented all of Egypt’s leaders from the greatest to the least important (see Isaiah 9:14-15).
An upraised fist (literally waving the hand) was a threatening motion.

five of Egypt’s cities: This is probably just a way of saying “a number of cities” (see also Isaiah 17:6; Isaiah 30:17). • Jews living in Egypt after the destruction of Jerusalem spoke Hebrew, here called the language of Canaan. • Heliopolis was devoted to Re, the sun god. At a time when Judah was resisting the Lord, Isaiah envisioned the Egyptians following the Lord.

This altar or monument refers either to the temple that was built by Jews at Elephantine in Egypt (500 BC), to some other Jewish place of worship, or perhaps to a memorial the Egyptians constructed in devotion to the Lord.
The new Egypt would receive a place in God’s purposes together with Assyria and Israel.

The altar (Isaiah 19:19) would be a sign and a witness of the Egyptians’ religious connection with Israel (see Isaiah 19:24-25). • God answers the prayers of those who cry to the Lord for help. • The Lord is a savior; he would protect the Egyptians even as he protected Jerusalem from the Assyrians.

strike Egypt: The Hebrew verb used here is the same as the one used for the tenth plague (Exodus 12:13, Exodus 12:23, Exodus 12:27), bringing up associations of what God did during the Exodus. • The Lord, who brings a plague, can also bring healing. • he will listen to their pleas and heal them: This expresses a covenantal relationship between the Lord and Egypt (see Isaiah 65:24).

Traditionally, Egypt and Assyria were enemies of one another and of Israel. They were idolatrous to the core, but they would leave behind their enmity and their idols to worship the true God. • In the rugged terrain of the ancient Near East, a highway provided a means for safe, easy travel and trade (see Isaiah 11:16; Isaiah 35:8; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 62:10).
Israel will be . . . a blessing in fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

Two designations usually reserved for Israel, my people and the land I have made (see Isaiah 29:22; Isaiah 32:18), are applied here to foreign nations. The Lord promised to regard those from the nations who turn to him as his special possession (Isaiah 63:17).
Sargon of Assyria is Sargon II (721–705 BC). • Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities that rebelled against Assyria in 713 BC.
Ashdod’s reliance on Egypt and Ethiopia was useless. As a complement to his words, Isaiah walked about exposed and barefoot, a symbolic action for what God would do.

Prophets characteristically wore burlap or other rough clothing as a sign of mourning over the sins of the people (see 2 Kgs 1:8; Mark 1:6). • naked: That is, exposed in some way, possibly even completely nude.
This symbolic event took place some three years before the fall of Ashdod (see Isaiah 20:2). Through it, Isaiah became an object lesson for the people (see Isaiah 8:18).
Philistia’s downfall was a warning to the people of Judah, who also relied on Egypt and other alliances rather than on God.

concerning Babylon—the desert by the sea: This description of Babylon was perhaps an ironic way to say that the land was physically lush but spiritually desolate. • Disaster . . . from the desert: Literally from the desert, from the terrifying land (cp. Deuteronomy 8:15).

I see: The prophet personalized Babylon’s experience, which intensifies his poetry, as does the terse language and the repetition of similar sounds, such as the betrayer betraying (Hebrew habboged boged) and the destroyer destroying (Hebrew hashoded shoded; also in Isaiah 33:1). • The Elamites lived to the northeast of Babylon. Along with the Medes, they were archrivals of the Babylonians. • I will make an end to all the groaning Babylon caused: Babylon had caused groaning by attacking and enslaving many nations. It is likely that the Elamites and Medes played a part in the overthrow of Babylon in 539 BC (Isaiah 21:9).
I grow faint . . . I am too afraid: Through his vision, Isaiah experienced the terror of the Babylonian people (see also Daniel 8:27; Daniel 10:16-17).
The riders were messengers who reported what had taken place on the battlefield.

Babylon is fallen, fallen: Assyrian king Sennacherib destroyed the city of Babylon in 689 BC. The final fall of Babylon was in 539 BC. In Scripture, Babylon represents all the ungodly power structures of this world, including nations and kingdoms that do not submit to God and his word. The apostle John gave hope with his prophecy that all Babylons will fall (Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:2). • All the idols of Babylon lie broken: False gods could not save the Babylonians (see Isaiah 46:1-2).

O my people: The focus shifted back to the people of Judah. • Judah would be oppressed (threshed and winnowed) by the Babylonians but Babylon, too, would fall. • I have told you everything: The prophet had been faithful in his duty to report what the Lord revealed to him.
