Edom: Hebrew Seir, which was the mountainous area of Edom. • how much longer until morning: Edom’s suffering would be a long ordeal. The Assyrians were dominant in the ancient Near East during the 700s and 600s BC.

These two prophecies pertain to Edom and Arabia, located in the territory between Babylon and Israel. These outlying regions suffered under Assyrian domination, and like Judah, they would not be able to rest under Babylon’s oppressive regime.
Morning is coming, but it would mark the beginning of another oppressive era. Because the Babylonians were on the horizon, night will soon return.

Dedan was a tribe in Arabia (see Ezekiel 27:20; Ezekiel 38:13). • Caravans would hide in the deserts of Arabia from attacks by the Assyrians and Babylonians, both of whom harassed the Arabian tribes (see Isaiah 21:1-10; Jeremiah 49:28-29).
Cp. Jeremiah 49:28-33.
Tema was an oasis in Arabia on a main trade route from Babylon.
Assyrian weapons of war such as the drawn sword and the bent bow were highly advanced compared to the primitive weapons used by desert peoples.
Kedar was an Arabian tribe that had great wealth and possessions (see Isaiah 60:7; Ezekiel 27:21).
Only a few . . . will survive: Cp. Isaiah 10:22; Isaiah 14:30; Isaiah 16:14; Isaiah 24:6, Isaiah 24:13; Isaiah 37:32.

concerning Jerusalem—the Valley of Vision: The meaning of the Hebrew phrase is uncertain. Assuming that it refers to Jerusalem (see Isaiah 22:5), it is ironic: Jerusalem sits atop a hill, and visions were not typically thought to originate in a valley. Similarly, Jerusalem was proud of its self-perceived religious vision, but its inhabitants were spiritually blind (see Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 42:18).

The prophet rebukes the people for their excitement over the Assyrian retreat (701 BC). They did not foresee that the Babylonian army would later (in 586 BC) complete what the Assyrians failed to do, namely, the destruction of Jerusalem.
This message addresses the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38; 2 Kgs 18:17–19:37) and perhaps the people’s preparation for the subsequent Babylonian siege in 588–586 BC.

The reveling city was full of feasting and drinking (Isaiah 22:13; see Isaiah 23:7; Isaiah 32:13), probably in response to the Assyrian retreat. Now a new threat approaches—the Babylonian siege (586 BC). • The people died not in battle but by famine and disease. Siege warfare left the inhabitants of the city cut off from needed agricultural resources and in a terrible sanitation and health crisis.
Leaders might try to flee, but they would not escape (see 2 Kgs 25:4-6).
Leave me alone to weep: Isaiah mourned the victims and the decimation of his people (see Isaiah 6:13).
Jerusalem’s walls were broken by the invading Babylonians, who breached them with battering rams (2 Kgs 25:4).
The defeat of Judah would be a manifestation of the yet-future day of the Lord (see study note on 2:5-22). Jerusalem would be impotent in the day of disaster.
Elamites: Elam was to the east of Babylon and would later play a role in Babylon’s defeat (see Isaiah 21:2; also Jeremiah 49:34-39). • The actual location of Kir is unknown (see also Amos 1:5).
The Kidron and Hinnom valleys were located to the east and south of Jerusalem.
to the armory: This magnificent building was both an armory and a storage place for valuables (see Isaiah 39:2; 1 Kgs 7:2-6).

The inhabitants of Jerusalem planned for war by counting weapons, checking walls, and preparing a water supply. However, the people did not consider God’s plans (see Isaiah 13:1–14:23). Although Hezekiah was very prominent in these efforts, the second person verbs are plural. Isaiah was apparently not singling out Hezekiah, as he did Hezekiah’s father Ahaz (Isaiah 7:1-4).

Jerusalem (literally the city of David): Calling Jerusalem “the city of David” evokes memories of Israel’s greatest king and God’s blessing upon him and the nation (see also Isaiah 60:14). • You store up water in the lower pool: Hezekiah expended great energy in ensuring a constant supply of water (see Isaiah 22:11; 2 Kgs 20:20).
Judah’s feasting and disobedience resulted in a prophecy of judgment.

you will never be forgiven for this sin: The people of Judah added sin upon sin to the point that God would justly condemn them. This foreshadowed the Exile; although it took place in 586 BC, Isaiah was already anticipating it in 701 BC.

The actions of Shebna represent among the populace a lack of confidence in God’s ability to rescue Jerusalem from the Assyrian attack. • A palace administrator held the highest possible position in the royal court (see Isaiah 22:21-22).

Shebna and Eliakim were two royal officials in King Hezekiah’s court (see 2 Kgs 18:18; 19:2). Apparently assuming that death at the hands of the Assyrians was inevitable, Shebna planned for an ostentatious burial place (Isaiah 22:16). Although the rebuke of Shebna preceded Assyria’s siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see Isaiah 22:19-21; Isaiah 36:3), it connects well with the admonitions of Isaiah 22:1-13 regarding the ensuing Babylonian siege.
Shebna was building a beautiful tomb . . . a monument. This lavish burial place was intended to last for centuries.
toss you away into a distant, barren land: Shebna would not find a resting place or have a memorial (cp. Isaiah 14:11-20). • your glorious chariots: In his high position, Shebna had lived in luxury.

drive you out of office: Shebna (Isaiah 22:15) was demoted to court secretary by the time of Jerusalem’s siege, when Eliakim (Isaiah 22:20) was the palace administrator (Isaiah 36:3). Eliakim was a true servant of the Lord.
A leader is like a father to the people when he truly cares for them and addresses their needs. In contrast, Shebna was concerned only for himself.

The key to the house of David represents a high position of honor in the royal court (see also Revelation 3:7). • When he opens doors . . . when he closes doors: The officer with the highest position has sole authority in giving access to the king (cp. Matthew 16:19).
I will pull out the nail: Even godly Eliakim would not be able to save Judah or David’s dynasty from God’s judgment. The people of Judah would go into exile more than a century later (Isaiah 39:6-7).

The ships of Tarshish plied the sea between the Phoenician coast and the port of Tarshish in Spain (see Isaiah 2:16; Isaiah 23:6). • rumors you heard in Cyprus: Cyprus was the last port of call for sailors coming home from Spain before the final leg of their journey to Tyre.

Tyre was a prosperous seaport northwest of Israel. The relationship between Judah and Tyre went back to the time of David and Solomon (1 Kgs 5:8-9). Tyre, with its proximity to plentiful forests and to the Mediterranean Sea, was one of the commercial centers of the ancient Near East. Its fleets were renowned, and its colonies brought it great prestige and riches. The city came under repeated attack by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Macedonians, and it fell to Alexander the Great in 332 BC. Isaiah not only prophesied the end of Tyre but by implication warned all whose wealth and earthly securities lead to pride instead of dependence on God (see Isaiah 2:12-16; Matthew 11:21).
Sidon was a Phoenician port to the north of Tyre. • Tyre’s commercial network of traders was extensive.

Fish, agricultural produce, flax, and linen were all harvests from along the Nile (see ch Isaiah 19:1-25). • Tyre was known as the marketplace of the world, comparable to modern cities like New York, Hong Kong, or London.

Part of the great port city of Tyre was on an island. The island city was a fortress of the sea, but it fell in 332 BC. • I am childless; I have no sons or daughters: This metaphor was a judgment on Tyre’s colonial ports around the Mediterranean Sea. In the ancient world, to reach old age without having children was considered a terrible fate (see Isaiah 49:21; Isaiah 54:1).
Egypt depended on the ships from Tyre for the export of its products (see Isaiah 23:3).
The Lord had brought this disaster on Tyre (Isaiah 23:9). • Through commercial links, Tyre had created wealth for itself and its trading partners; in this sense, Tyre was a great creator of kingdoms.

Sweep over the land like the flooding Nile: This difficult phrase means either (1) that the sailors who had returned from Tarshish were being invited to loot ruined Tyre; or (2) that the people of Tarshish were forced to move back to their agricultural fields to make their living (instead of trading) now that Tyre had been destroyed.
Phoenicia was the region north of Israel. Tyre and Sidon were its main cities.
Babylonia was stripped and looted by the Assyrians under Sennacherib (689 BC); eventually it rose to be a mighty empire once again.
There was hope for Tyre.
Metaphorically, Tyre was a prostitute because of its indifferent willingness to sell anything to anyone (cp. Revelation 17:2; Revelation 18:3, Revelation 18:12-13).

Even though Tyre’s earnings came from unrighteous commerce, the profits will be given to the Lord rather than being squandered. • There will be good food and fine clothing for the Lord’s priests. The theme of the wealth of the nations being brought to the Lord in Jerusalem is more fully developed in Isaiah 60:5-11; Isaiah 61:6.

destroy the earth and make it a vast wasteland: There is a play here on the Hebrew words baqaq (destroy) and balaq (make a wasteland). The devastation will begin with Judah and be extended to the whole world (see 1 Pet 4:17). • All the earth will be destroyed, the people as well as national political structures.
Here the judgments described in chs Isaiah 13:1–23:18 are extended to the creation at large.

This section is often referred to as the “Little Apocalypse” because of its similarities to the book of Revelation. In these chapters Isaiah takes readers out of the present into a vision of the future world. The universal imagery of the Little Apocalypse makes it difficult to assign the events described to any precise historical situation. That means that these chapters cannot be used to outline a sequence of events or create a historical blueprint for the future. Instead, the imagery is intended to create an impressionistic drama of an unfolding world that is both like and unlike the present. The combination of aspects of the old era with aspects of the new era (for instance, people of Zion will all be righteous [new], but still long for their redemption [old]) is consistent with the New Testament concept of the future age breaking into and overlapping with the present evil age (2 Cor 4:4; Galatians 1:4). Peter, for example, wrote of believers as living in the last days (1 Pet 1:12; 2 Pet 3:3) even though the last day remains yet future (2 Pet 3:10).

earth . . . dries up . . . land wastes away and withers: The prophets often used the imagery of a drought to get the attention of people who live off the land (see also Jeremiah 23:10; Joel 1:12; Amos 1:2).
All humanity is guilty (Romans 3:23) and under condemnation (see Isaiah 59:1-15). Judgment is likened to a failed grape harvest that brings drinking and feasting to a halt.

Isaiah was probably referring to the everlasting covenant that God made with all humanity through Noah (Genesis 9:8-17). The prophet saw a parallel with the wickedness in his day and the wickedness of the pre-flood world.
The effect of sin is so great that no earthly thing or action can adequately atone for it. Hope ultimately lies in God himself. God has reconciled the world to himself in Christ (Colossians 1:19-20).
Merrymakers will sigh and mourn because they are dependent on wine for pleasure.
Tambourines and melodious chords of the harp represent good times (see Isaiah 5:12; Revelation 18:22).
city writhes in chaos: With normal levels of urban disarray being raised to chaotic and dangerous disorder, people will be forced to seek refuge in locked homes.
Gladness has been banished from the land, not by edict, but because there is no reason to celebrate.

stray olives left on the tree: The remnant will include godly people both from Israel (see Isaiah 17:6) and from other nations. • The theme of the remnant is common in Isaiah (see “The Remnant” Theme Note; see also Isaiah 10:22; Isaiah 14:30; Isaiah 16:14; Isaiah 24:6; Isaiah 37:32).

In spite of wailing and ruin, the sound of praise is heard from all directions. Even while still experiencing the pain of the devastation of the old world, the godly will respond with joyous expectation for the new world.

But my heart is heavy with grief: The prophets were well acquainted with the emotional pain brought on by the sin of their people and its consequences (see Isaiah 15:5; Isaiah 21:4; Jeremiah 15:10; Micah 1:8). • Although aspects of the new world are present, the deceit of the old world still prevails for a time.

No one can escape the day of the Lord (see study note on 2:5-22). • Destruction falls like rain from the heavens (literally the floodgates of heaven are opened): The imagery is like the flood in Noah’s time (see study note on Gen 7:11-12). • the foundations of the earth shake: An earthquake is characteristic of a theophany, a physical manifestation of God’s presence (see also Isaiah 6:4; Isaiah 13:13; Isaiah 19:1).

The phrase translated gods (Hebrew tseba’ hammarom, “armed host of the heavens”) might refer to pagan gods represented by the stars. It might also refer to the angels or even demons (Revelation 12:4, Revelation 12:9). Judgment will extend to all parts of creation (Isaiah 13:13; Isaiah 34:5; see Ephesians 6:11-12).
put in prison . . . punished: See also 2 Pet 2:4; Revelation 9:2, Revelation 9:11; Revelation 17:8.
Isaiah here praises God for protecting the needy (see Isaiah 12:1-6).
The second part of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on 24:1–27:13) describes praise for God’s judgment (Isaiah 25:1-5, Isaiah 25:11-12) and salvation (Isaiah 25:6-9).
Assyria and Egypt were strong . . . ruthless nations, but in the future they will exalt God rather than their own power.

In Jerusalem: Literally On this mountain—that is, the mountain of the Lord (see Isaiah 2:2; Isaiah 24:23): This does not refer to a geographical city but to Zion, the eternal city of God (see Isaiah 1:8, Isaiah 1:27).
The banquet is a symbol of God’s providing richly for all those who will receive his gracious invitation (Revelation 3:20-21; Revelation 19:9).

He will swallow up death forever: Isaiah’s hope was God’s power over sin and sin’s devastating results. In the New Testament this promise is realized in Jesus Christ (1 Cor 15:54). • The Lord’s presence will be a source of eternal comfort; he will wipe away all tears (see Revelation 21:4).
The new community of God’s people will respond in joy and faith. When the enemy is defeated, God’s people will be free forever.

on Jerusalem: Literally on this mountain. • Moab (see Isaiah 15:1–16:14) here represents the nations under judgment, those who trust only themselves (see Isaiah 34:5-17). • like straw trampled down: The people would be helpless and dying in the most degrading circumstances.
Isaiah used the image of a swimmer forcibly kept under water to illustrate that Moab’s people are hopelessly doomed and their human pride will be conquered.

Our city refers to Zion, the eternal city of God, where the Lord is present to protect and bless his people (see Isaiah 1:8, Isaiah 1:27; see also Psalm 46:1-11). Zion stands in direct contrast to the “mighty cities” of the nations (Isaiah 25:2; Isaiah 26:5), which are helpless and are brought down to “ruins.” • The walls of God’s salvation protectively enclose his people; no one can hurt them again.
The new community of God’s people is likened to the citizens of a city, securely held together by the Lord. They are righteous, faithful, peaceful, and trusting.
This section of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on 24:1–27:13) is a song of praise and a prayer for redemption.
Open access is given to all who, like God and his Messiah, are righteous and faithful. The citizens of true Zion are committed to the Lord.
A perfect peace, marked by harmony, quietness, and confidence, is a benefit of the new creation.
The proud and arrogant are often characterized as exalting themselves (see Isaiah 2:11-12), whereas God humbles them.
Justice finally occurs when the needy walk all over the ruins of the city where the proud have perished.

God will do what is right for those who walk in his way, even if they have to suffer a while longer (see Isaiah 24:16). One day, they will experience harmony and integrity (see Proverbs 2:8-9; Proverbs 15:19).

The godly pray for the end of oppression and the full establishment of God’s kingdom. Isaiah encouraged the godly to persevere as they wait for their final vindication and the resurrection of the body.

we show our trust (see Isaiah 26:3-4; literally we wait for you): Waiting involves trust in the Lord and longing for his redemption. • People express their commitment to God by obeying his laws; mere lip service is not sufficient.
I search . . . I earnestly seek: Cp. Psalm 63:1.
God has shown kindness to the wicked. Although they deserve judgment (see also Romans 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9), he has been patient and forbearing and has blessed them. However, time will run out one day.
An upraised fist expresses anger and the threat of judgment (see also Isaiah 19:16). • Fire was often an image for God’s judgment.

This verse is a confident expression of thanks for God’s blessings. In Isaiah’s time, during King Hezekiah’s prosperous reign, the borders of the nation of Israel were extended, and people gave glory to God for his great deeds.

While waiting for God’s salvation (Isaiah 26:1), the godly were in distress and longed for their vindication. They prayed beneath the burden of God’s discipline. In Hezekiah’s time, Judah was in distress when Sennacherib attacked and destroyed the whole nation except for Jerusalem.
The imagery of a pregnant woman in childbirth describes the nation’s pain when Assyrian king Sennacherib attacked it in 701 BC (see Isaiah 37:3).
Only God can give salvation and bring life (see Isaiah 59:9-15).

those who die . . . will live: There is hope for the remnant. Some hold the minimal interpretation that this means the people would be restored to the land after the Exile (see Ezekiel 37:11-12) or that the Lord would preserve Jerusalem (see Isaiah 29:4, Isaiah 29:6-8). More likely it refers to the resurrection of the body from the grave (see Isaiah 25:7-8). The Old Testament has little to say about the resurrection, but this text anticipates fuller development in the New Testament (see 1 Cor 15:12-58).
God will punish the wicked, so the godly should go home and stay out of the way.
The wicked retain power now, but their oppressive rule will end in the day of the Lord’s wrath, when he will punish them for their sins.

Israel adapted the imagery of Leviathan to refer to evil powers that oppose God. Leviathan’s death symbolizes the end of evil, Satan, the demonic, and the dominion of forces hostile to God (see Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 74:14; Psalm 104:7-9, Psalm 104:26; see also the serpent in Genesis 3:1-24; Revelation 12:1-18; Revelation 13:1-18; Revelation 16:13; Revelation 20:2, Revelation 20:10).
The Song of the Fruitful Vineyard, in which the vineyard represents God’s people (cp. Isaiah 5:1-7).

God identifies himself as the Lord of the covenant to assure his people that what he says and does is reliable (see Exodus 6:2-3). The phrase is used many times throughout Isaiah. • watch . . . watering . . . watch: The Lord will provide even greater care and protection for his ultimate vineyard than he did for Israel, his first vineyard (see Isaiah 5:1-2).
God expects all his people to turn to him and to trust him for help. • Let them make peace with me is God’s offer of reconciliation for his people.

Jacob’s descendants will take root and the remnant will increase (Isaiah 37:31; cp. Isaiah 5:24; Isaiah 14:30; for application to the Messiah, see Isaiah 11:1, Isaiah 11:10). • fill the whole earth: The fulfillment of this prophecy extends beyond the restoration of Israel from exile to the second coming of the Lord Jesus. It includes all the righteous children of God—Jews and Gentiles—who suffer but remain obedient as they wait for the fullness of redemption (see Isaiah 26:18; John 15:1-8).
Despite being God’s covenant people, Israel was struck and punished like any other wicked nation. However, Israel was not completely destroyed; a remnant remained.
Isaiah reminded readers of the reasons for the Exile and judgment: Israel’s sinfulness, God’s righteous judgment, and the absence of divine compassion.

The Assyrians exiled large numbers of citizens from the northern kingdom of Israel when Samaria fell in 722 BC. The Babylonians exiled many from Judah from 605 to 586 BC. • Storms from the east were known for their destructive effects (see Job 27:21; Job 38:24; Jeremiah 4:11).

God’s justice requires him to punish sin. That punishment is designed to correct behavior and to purify. Being conquered and exiled wasThe Exile occurred so that to purge Israel’s wickedness and to take away all her sin (see Romans 11:27). • This was to be the end of all the pagan worship in Israel, including the incense altars and the poles that were used in worshiping the goddess Asherah.
Places previously associated with human power and accomplishment would be ruined to the extent that animals would graze in them.
The people were outside of God’s covenantal care; they foolishly turned away from him.

Yet: God’s withholding of mercy from Israel (Isaiah 27:11) will be temporary. • from the Euphrates River . . . to the Brook of Egypt: God’s remnant will return from Assyria and Egypt to the territory that God promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18; see 1 Kgs 4:21).
The great trumpet was used to gather the people (see Matthew 24:31).
The drunks of Israel epitomized pride, spiritual complacency, and scorn for God and his commands. • Unlike Jerusalem, Samaria was in a fertile valley.
The glory of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, is here contrasted with the glory of the Lord. This section represents the first of the six woes (What sorrow . . .).

This section is connected by a series of six threats of judgment or woes (cp. Isaiah 5:8-23). Apart from the initial address to Samaria in Isaiah 28:1-13, the remainder of the section is addressed to Judah, especially because of their inclination to trust Egypt to rescue them from Assyria (Isaiah 30:2).

the Lord will send: The covenant God will act against his own people, whose behavior had effectively disqualified them as God’s people (see Hosea 1:9). • The mighty army is that of the Assyrians, who destroyed Samaria in 722 BC.

In the future, after God’s judgment has purged his people, he will restore a righteous remnant, transforming the desires and character of his people. Samaria will no longer be the source of Israel’s pride; instead, they will glory in the Lord, their true crown.
The priests and prophets led the people astray. • Intoxicating beverages such as wine and alcohol were prohibited for priests while fulfilling their duties (Leviticus 10:9).
The focus returns to the lamentable present situation in Israel (and Judah). The leaders and people will be ensnared by their own schemes.
The people had become hardened to God’s revelation (1 Cor 14:21).

God will have to speak through circumstances such as hardship, exile, and death in order to get through to his hardened people. • a strange language: In the New Testament, Paul applied this text to the spiritual gift of tongues as a sign of judgment to unbelievers (see 1 Cor 14:21-22).
Had his people listened, God’s revelation would have led them to rest (see Isaiah 48:18-19). But they would not listen because of their hard hearts (Isaiah 65:12).

one line at a time, one line at a time, a little here, and a little there: The Hebrew here is difficult to understand. The words might be intentional nonsense to illustrate the point that the people were so spiritually blind that God’s clearest revelation was nonsense to them (see Isaiah 6:9-10).

After having pronounced judgment on Samaria (Isaiah 28:1-13), Isaiah now pronounces judgment on Jerusalem. The leaders of Judah are accused of being as blind as those in the northern kingdom of Israel.

cheat death (literally have made a covenant with death) . . . dodge the grave: There are two interpretive possibilities: (1) The people had sold themselves to the Canaanite god of death, Mot, in return for his supposed protection. (2) The prophet was being sarcastic; the people thought their various political and economic moves guaranteed their personal security, but they had actually destroyed themselves. • lies and deception: The leaders did not think of themselves as deceptive, but they were.

The Lord himself is the reliable foundation stone in Jerusalem, a precious cornerstone of the true city of God. There would be real hope in Jerusalem if the leaders and the people would only turn to him. If they would trust in God, they would be secure in the most terrible storm or the most devastating earthquake (see Isaiah 8:14; Psalm 118:22; Matthew 7:24-27; Matthew 21:42; see the application to Jesus Christ, Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11; 1 Cor 3:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Pet 2:4-7).
The Lord judges people on their works, which reveal the presence or absence of living faith (for justice and righteousness, see Isaiah 1:21-23).
The bed. . . . The blankets: The leaders were ill-prepared for God’s coming in judgment.
as he did . . . at Mount Perazim: See 2 Sam 5:20. • God had rescued Israel through a hailstorm at Gibeon (Joshua 10:10-12), but now he would turn against them.
Listen to me: The analogy that follows was written as a wisdom poem, with Isaiah calling on his audience to pay careful attention and to discern what is right.
A farmer knows that there are right and wrong ways to do things, but the leaders of Judah were not that intelligent.
The Lord has a variety of means (a heavy sledge . . . a light stick) for accomplishing his purposes. There are degrees of judgment.
he doesn’t keep on pounding it: This process would end; after judgment would come redemption.
wonderful teacher (or counselor; see Isaiah 9:6): God’s people should learn wisdom about God’s ways, as the farmer has done.
Ariel was another name for Mount Zion (Isaiah 29:8); it probably means altar of God.
In the Assyrian siege, the Lord would be fighting against Jerusalem, but he would force the Assyrians to abandon Jerusalem in his own time.
This is the second of the six woes (What sorrow . . .).
The Lord himself would come against Jerusalem, surrounding and attacking it.
God’s goal was to destroy the sinful pride of the people of Jerusalem. Their voice would rise as if from the grave. Through the Assyrians, God would humble his people, but he would not abandon them.

will act for you (literally you will be visited): God would bring rescue for his people. • thunder and earthquake . . . storm and consuming fire: These phenomena indicate a theophany (see study note on 5:25).
The Assyrians’ sudden lifting of the siege came like a dream . . . like a vision in the night. God would save Judah and judge Assyria.
Like a hungry or thirsty person, the Assyrians could taste the victory over Jerusalem. Yet they never became victorious.
Jerusalem’s blindness kept its people from understanding God’s plan.

a spirit of deep sleep: The people’s folly was reinforced by God’s judgment on them (cp. Romans 1:24-32; Romans 11:8); they had no perception of reality. • Prophets were also sometimes called visionaries. Neither the people nor their prophets would understand what God was doing (Isaiah 6:9-10).

These people used pious-sounding language in their prayers and talk (see Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6-7), but they did not truly honor God. • In their hearts, they were not committed to the Lord at all. • In their worship, they followed man-made rules and regulations rather than God’s word.
Human wisdom . . . intelligence . . . will disappear (see 1 Cor 1:19). The prophet had already spoken of the failure of Egypt’s wise men (Isaiah 19:11-12); even Judah’s wise men would blunder.

Their plans might refer to the advice that royal counselors were giving Hezekiah, who at first attempted to free himself from Assyria by making alliances with Egypt (715 or 701 BC). • The people were conspiring to commit evil deeds in secret, but God saw everything.
This threat of coming judgment is the third of the six woes (see study note on 28:1–33:24). It begins with judgment but moves to a vision of creation being renewed and of the wicked coming to an end.

Potter . . . clay: The Lord’s sovereignty is beyond challenge. Scripture does not discourage asking God hard questions, but there is no place for resistance to God’s will (see Isaiah 10:15; Isaiah 45:9; Isaiah 64:8; Romans 9:20). • He didn’t make me: Such claims against God demonstrate a total unwillingness to recognize God’s intimate involvement with every aspect of a person’s life.
The forests of Lebanon are usually an image of luxuriant growth (see Isaiah 2:13; Isaiah 14:8), but here they represent desolation.
The people were deaf and blind in heart and spirit (see Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 42:18; Isaiah 43:8). Yet humanity and all of creation would be renewed (see Isaiah 35:1-5).

The false testimony that led to the oppression of the poor through trickery in the courts of Isaiah’s era would end. Because of God’s work in their hearts, the people would turn from their sinful behavior of the past.

Abraham was the father of all Israel (see Genesis 12:1-3; see also Galatians 3:29). • Rescued from human abuse and God’s judgment, the people would no longer be ashamed; their disgrace resulted from the apparent failure of what they had trusted (see Psalm 71:1; 1 Pet 2:6).
The prophecy of woe, which began at Isaiah 29:15, now ends with a prophecy of salvation.

The wisdom of the people of Judah was not directed by God’s Spirit (cp. Isaiah 11:2); instead, they had formed alliances that God did not approve of. Although the Assyrian attack on Jerusalem was overwhelming, making an alliance with Egypt demonstrated that the leaders of Judah depended on human resources for their protection rather than on God. Fortunately, Hezekiah later had a change of heart (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38).
This prophecy was against Judah’s dependence on Egypt. It is the fourth of the six woes (see study note on 28:1–33:24).

After threatening Judah with judgment because of their stubbornness and their reliance on Egypt (Isaiah 30:1-17), God again committed himself to deal compassionately with his people and to break the power of their enemies.
Zoan: See Isaiah 19:11. The location of Hanes is uncertain.

Caravans moved from Judah through the Negev and the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt to avoid the main coast road that was under Assyrian control. It was a dangerous region, filled with lions and poisonous snakes. People would risk their lives to make a worthless alliance. • Being weighed down with riches might refer to money being sent to Egypt to buy that nation’s help.
This taunt was against those who were busy trying to please the Egyptians in order to get Egypt’s military support.

Harmless Dragon: In ancient mythology, Rahab was the enemy of the good gods and was depicted in fearsome terms, somewhat like a giant crocodile (see Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9; Job 41:1-34). By saying that Egypt was harmless, the prophet meant that it would be of no help to Judah.

God instructed the prophet to write down the vision for future generations. The present generation was rebellious; they rejected God’s word in favor of the false prophets’ fantasies (see Isaiah 8:16-17).
Stop telling us: The people of Judah did not want to be confronted about sin or judgment.

The whole society accepted oppression and lies. People reinforced each other’s delusions, so it was considered acceptable to trust that Egypt would protect them from Assyria, even though that was a lie. It was also considered legal and legitimate to oppress the poor by taking their land.
Judgment would suddenly overtake the people of Judah because they were content with their fantasy world, and they refused God’s path to rest and quietness.

The people of Judah needed to repent of their sinful ways (Isaiah 30:12-14), returning to the Lord, in order to be rescued. • Trust in the Lord would bring quietness and confidence, unlike their frantic negotiations with Egypt.
Judah’s reliance on Egypt to supply swift horses (see Psalm 33:17) amounted to a rejection of God’s help and threatened to bring about its fall.

One . . . Five: This curse is the opposite of God’s blessing for obedience (Leviticus 26:8; Deuteronomy 32:30). • The Assyrians had dominated the rest of the land of Judah, leaving Jerusalem isolated like a lonely flagpole on a hill.

A faithful God would restore righteous order to the world by punishing the wicked and rescuing his people from them (see Isaiah 1:27; Psalm 96:10-12). • God blesses those who wait; faithful people do not rush ahead of him to solve their own problems but instead rely on his power and goodness.
This prophecy of salvation includes promises that directed Israel’s attention away from their present adversity to the glorious future awaiting the children of God.

This was probably a challenge and promise to Hezekiah during the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (see chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38). If he would just trust in God, his people would weep no more. • The Lord cares for the needs of his people; when they ask for something, he will surely respond.

adversity for food and suffering for drink: A city under enemy siege for a long time would eventually be overcome by starvation and disease. God did not intend that this disaster should destroy the people of Jerusalem, rather that it would be a tool to teach them.
The people’s own ears will hear and follow God’s instructions (see Isaiah 6:9-10; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 35:5).
One aspect of Hezekiah’s reforms was to remove silver idols and other idolatry of Ahaz’s era and to call the people back to the worship of the God of Israel (2 Kgs 18:4-5; 2 Chr 29).
The people of Judah would again enjoy covenant blessings rather than curses (see Leviticus 26:4).
The Lord who struck his people would also heal them and cure the wounds he gave them.
In this prophecy of judgment against the nations, Isaiah foretold that Assyria’s power would be broken by God’s strong arm, not by the Egyptians.
like a flood up to the neck: Assyria’s destruction would be as devastating as their invasion of Judah (see Isaiah 8:8).

His mighty arm presents an image of strength that echoes God’s victory over the Egyptians in the Exodus (Isaiah 63:12; see Exodus 15:6). • devouring flames . . . huge hailstones: Such phenomena are associated with God’s appearance in a theophany (see study note on Isa 5:25).
royal scepter: The Lord, the true King, would be victorious over the threatening Assyrian king.

tambourines and harps: Instruments formerly silenced in judgment (Isaiah 24:8) would again be used by God’s people; this time, the people would celebrate the Lord’s goodness rather than becoming spiritually complacent (see Isaiah 5:12).
Topheth was a pagan altar in the valley of Ben-Hinnom outside Jerusalem where child sacrifices were offered to the Ammonite god Molech by burning (2 Kgs 23:9-10).
What sorrow: This is the fifth of the six woes (see study note on 28:1–33:24). • Looking to the Lord implies seeking his guidance with a worshipful attitude (see Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 105:3-4).

Isaiah delivered another vision regarding Judah’s negotiations with Egypt, which probably took place in 705–701 BC. During that time, the conquering Assyrians were on the move, threatening Judah. At first, Hezekiah tried political and military means to avert being totally conquered (see 2 Kgs 18:13-16).
This prophecy concerned God’s protection of Jerusalem and its rescue from the Assyrians.
princes will flee: This was fulfilled when Sennacherib fled to Nineveh after God destroyed 185,000 troops (see Isaiah 37:36-37). • God himself was the fire or flame that would devour Assyria.

a righteous king: The Messiah (Isaiah 11:1); the emphasis now is on righteous and wise leadership (Proverbs 8:20). • In Isaiah’s day, honest princes were few and far between (see Isaiah 3:1-6; Isaiah 28:7-19).

like a shelter . . . a refuge: The same words were also used to describe God’s protection (Isaiah 25:4) and his provision of life-giving water (Isaiah 41:18; Isaiah 43:19-20). The leaders would serve as God’s agents in blessing his people.
Only foolish people value fools and scoundrels as heroes (see also Isaiah 19:11, Isaiah 19:13; Isaiah 32:6-8).
Because they do not care about God’s standards of justice and righteousness, fools have no regard for those who are hungry or thirsty (see Isaiah 1:17; Isaiah 58:7, Isaiah 58:10).
smooth tricks . . . crooked schemes: See Proverbs 6:12, Proverbs 6:18; Proverbs 16:27; Proverbs 24:8-9.
The women of Jerusalem lie around in ease. Complacent in their high standard of life and low standard of morality, they put their trust in wealth and status to maintain their way of life.
This prophecy of judgment was against the complacent women of Jerusalem. God’s promises regarding the future did not justify continuing in sin.
In a short time: Assyria’s siege of Jerusalem (701 BC) was looming.

Burlap was worn to show . . . grief, especially when mourning (see Psalm 30:11). The Assyrian conquest of the farmlands of Judah and most of its cities (except Jerusalem) would cause rich people in the large cities to mourn.
Jerusalem was eventually destroyed, but by the Babylonians, not the Assyrians (for a prediction of this, see Isaiah 39:1-8).

The Spirit would transform the nation into a godly community and bring in an era of justice and righteousness (see also Joel 2:28-32). The Spirit is connected to the Messiah (Isaiah 11:1) and the servant (Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 61:1). • wilderness . . . bountiful crops: When the people are transformed, nature will be too.

Being right with God and humans will bring peace (Hebrew shalom; see Isaiah 26:3; Isaiah 48:18; Isaiah 52:7; cp. James 3:18). Peace is more than the absence of conflict. It includes personal wholeness and does not depend on outside circumstances (see also Romans 5:1).

Living in safety and feeling at rest were blessings of Israel’s covenant with the Lord (see Leviticus 26:5-6), but the people’s sin had previously brought curses rather than blessings (cp. Isaiah 32:9-11).
the forest . . . the city: The godly would remain secure even with evidence of God’s judgment all around them.

This was the sixth threat of woe (see study note on 28:1–33:24). • Although the Hebrew text does not specifically name Assyria as the object of the prophecy in this chapter, Isaiah undoubtedly had Assyria in mind; they were the destroyer most immediately at hand when the prophecy was written. The prophecy applies, however, to any who seek to destroy God’s people; this included, but was not limited to, the Babylonians (see chs Isaiah 13:1–14:32). • When you are done betraying: Wicked nations often break political agreements with other nations when these contracts are no longer to their own advantage.
The godly community prayed for God to be merciful in response to the promise of Isaiah 30:18.
Sharon, Bashan, and Carmel were all fertile areas. Their desolation represents the destruction Assyria had inflicted on Israel.

In most passages, the Assyrians were turning other nations into worthless dry grass and stubble (see Isaiah 17:13; Isaiah 29:5; Isaiah 40:24; Isaiah 41:2). Here, ironically, they get a taste of their own medicine.

The godless were people who lived without regard for God and his law. • The image of a devouring fire came from God’s judgment of offenders during the wilderness journey (Exodus 24:17; Deuteronomy 4:24). God still expects people to worship him with reverence and awe (Hebrews 12:29).
A godly life provides evidence that an individual truly knows God (see Colossians 3:5-17; James 2:14-18; 1 Pet 1:14-16; 1 Jn 1:5-6).

The king is the human representative (Isaiah 32:1) of the Great King, God himself (Isaiah 33:22). • The land belonging to God’s people would appear to be without borders because the foreign enemies had been judged (Isaiah 54:3).
This vision is about God’s reign in Zion.
Assyrian officers brought great terror to Judah when the Assyrians defeated various cities around Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:13).
The strange, unknown language was the tongue of Assyria and later of Babylon (see Isaiah 28:11).
The people of Israel were the people of Zion (cp. Isaiah 33:20). • sick . . . the Lord will forgive their sins: See Isaiah 43:25.
This prophecy of judgment was against the nations at the terrifying day of the Lord (see study note on 2:5-22; see also Isaiah 63:1-6).
completely destroy: See Leviticus 27:28-29.
It was a disgrace for a corpse to remain unburied.
The heavens . . . stars: See also Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:30-31; Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24-25; 2 Pet 3:10-13; Revelation 6:13-14.
Edom here represents what all the nations would experience, just as Moab was singled out in ch Isaiah 25:1-12.
Bozrah was a city in Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea.

The Lord’s revenge refers to God’s wrathful but righteous vengeance against his enemies and the oppressors of his people on the day of the Lord. • Edom will be paid back: There will be retribution for Edom’s crimes against Judah (see also Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21; Obad; Malachi 1:3-5). Edom, with its history of treachery, would come to an end.
Edom’s judgment was similar to the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24; see also Jeremiah 49:17-18).
See also Revelation 14:11; Revelation 19:3.
The identification of some of these birds is uncertain, but they inhabited wild and deserted places and many were considered unclean (Deuteronomy 14:11-18).
Wild animals, night birds, and hostile plants with thorns and nettles created an eerie environment.

Search the book of the Lord: Isaiah’s prophecy was God’s witness to the truthfulness of his word. • The power of the Spirit enacts the Lord’s decrees, assuring that all prophecy comes together to be fulfilled as God promised.

God’s land would become like a wasteland, spiritually desolate and physically depleted. However, God would turn the desert into a garden (see also Isaiah 32:15), taking his people from exile to glory.
God will come to vindicate and transform his people. Instead of being deaf, blind, and lame (see Isaiah 6:10), the people will be pure, holy, and redeemed.

Lebanon . . . Mount Carmel . . . Sharon: There will be a reversal of earlier judgments (see Isaiah 2:13; Isaiah 10:34; Isaiah 29:17; Isaiah 33:9). • glory . . . splendor of our God: See also Isaiah 6:3; Isaiah 40:5.
Tired hands and weak knees express discouragement and anxiety (see Hebrews 12:12).

do not fear: The Lord here assures his people of his presence and purpose (see also Isaiah 7:4; Isaiah 10:24; Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 44:2; Isaiah 54:4). • The essence of the good news is that God is coming to save his people (see also Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 62:11). God’s coming brings spiritual transformation as well as rescue from enemies.

eyes . . . ears: There will be a transformation from spiritual blindness and deafness to understanding and knowing God (Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 32:3; Isaiah 42:7; see also Luke 7:22; Acts 26:18).
The lame . . . those who cannot speak: All disabilities will be removed (see Matthew 11:5; Matthew 12:22; Mark 7:37; Acts 3:7-8).

The imagery of the great road recalls Israel’s crossing through the Red Sea (Isaiah 51:10). • Only holy and undefiled people will share the Highway of Holiness. God’s goal in salvation is that humans will share in his character and act as he does (see Ephesians 5:1-2; 1 Pet 2:21).

Jerusalem: The prophecy extends beyond the return of Israel from exile to the final establishment of God’s kingdom on earth. It will be characterized by joy and gladness and the absence of sorrow and mourning (see also Isaiah 25:7; Isaiah 51:11; Revelation 21:4).

King Sennacherib of Assyria ruled from 705–681 BC. Hezekiah, like many other kings under Assyrian vassalage, had reasserted his independence when Sennacherib came to the throne in troubled circumstances. By 701 BC, the Assyrian king was ready to punish Hezekiah. Sennacherib recorded having conquered forty-six fortified cities and many villages, and having taken 200,146 captives. Hezekiah responded by attempting to appease Sennacherib (see 2 Kgs 18:14-16), but it was too late.

Jerusalem’s rescue from King Sennacherib of Assyria is a focal point of chs Isaiah 1:1–39:8. The Lord promised to rescue his people by remaining present with Jerusalem (see Isaiah 7:14) and by maintaining a remnant (see study note on 10:20). Even though much of the country was desolate and the population decimated because of their foolish alliance with Assyria (chs Isaiah 7:1–8:22), the Lord preserved his people from total conquest through Hezekiah, a godly king. Hezekiah faced the same test that Ahaz did, a test of trust (note the recurrence of words for trust in the Assyrian officer’s challenge in ch Isaiah 36:1-22). But Hezekiah has learned the lessons taught in chs Isaiah 13:1–35:10 and, at least initially, he passed the test. This narrative is duplicated in 2 Kgs 18:13–20:19.

Lachish was a city overlooking the low-lying hills to the west of Jerusalem. It had to be taken before the final attack on Jerusalem could be launched. • the aqueduct that feeds water into the upper pool: This was a pool on the north side of Jerusalem, not the Gihon Spring in the Kidron valley. • Isaiah had met Ahaz on this same road leading to the field where cloth is washed some thirty-three years earlier (see Isaiah 7:3). At that time he had challenged Ahaz to trust God. However, Ahaz trusted Assyria instead, and this desperate situation was a result. Now the challenge to trust God came from mocking, foreign lips (see Isaiah 28:11-13).
Eliakim eventually advanced in rank, while Shebna was demoted (see Isaiah 22:15-24).
Great king is a title similar to emperor.

The Assyrian chief of staff attempted to use intimidation to negotiate a settlement without bloodshed. In his first speech (Isaiah 36:4-10), he rightly argued against Egypt’s ability to rescue but wrongly charged Hezekiah with misplaced trust in the Lord. Strikingly, the Assyrian did not see the contest as being between the gods of Assyria and the Lord but rather between Sennacherib—the great king—and the Lord.
Who are you counting on: Judah had asked Egypt to help them (see Isaiah 30:1-5).

Egypt . . . is completely unreliable: Isaiah argued the same case, pointing to the Lord as the only reliable source of help (Isaiah 31:1-3, Isaiah 31:7; Isaiah 39:7). • A kind of reed that breaks easily grows near the Nile (see Ezekiel 29:6-7).

We are trusting in the Lord our God: Ironically, the Assyrian chief of staff knew about and played on Isaiah’s message (Isaiah 26:4; Isaiah 36:15; Isaiah 37:10). • Hezekiah showed his zeal for the Lord by tearing down the pagan shrines and altars (2 Kgs 18:4), but the Assyrians mistakenly thought Hezekiah had angered God in the process.
At this time, cavalry mounted on horses was the newest military technology. The Assyrian chief of staff was mocking the Judeans because he knew that Judah had no trained men who knew how to ride.
The Lord himself told us: It was common for a king to claim the approval of a deity in destroying other kingdoms. This claim was consistent with Isaiah’s prophecy in Isaiah 10:5-6.
Aramaic was the lingua franca used throughout the Assyrian Empire, understood by the elite but not by the common people of Judah.

In the Assyrian chief of staff’s second speech, he claimed that his nation’s gods were more powerful than the God of Judah (cp. Isaiah 10:9-10). God’s ability to rescue his people was at stake. In the ensuing drama, the Lord shocked the Assyrian with his power (Isaiah 37:36-37).
Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you: This public accusation against Hezekiah was intended to undermine the people’s confidence in him.
Hezekiah demonstrated a strong faith in the Lord, unlike Ahaz (ch Isaiah 7:1-25). Hezekiah’s faith would bring rescue, whereas Ahaz’s lack of faith brought him trouble (see Isaiah 7:9).

The Assyrian was tempting the people of Jerusalem with provisions that the Lord had promised to provide his obedient people (see Isaiah 1:19; Isaiah 37:30-35; Deuteronomy 8:7-9). It was a tempting offer, but a counterfeit. And it covered up the reality of exile that would have followed (Isaiah 36:17).

The populations of Hamath and Arpad had been relocated to Samaria, where the new local deities were the gods of Sepharvaim (2 Kgs 17:24). The logic of the argument made sense to an Assyrian. If the Assyrian gods defeated all the gods of the other nations and the God of the Israelite nation of Samaria, would they not also defeat the God of Judah?
Hezekiah responded to the threats by seeking the Lord’s favor. • The king tore his clothes and put on burlap as a sign of mourning and prayer.

perhaps . . . God has heard the Assyrian chief of staff . . . defy the living God: Hezekiah’s hope was not based on Judah’s or his own goodness, or the presence of the Temple in Jerusalem; instead, it was based on God responding to Assyria’s blasphemy.
God answered that he would deal with the Assyrians and rescue the remnant of his people from their distress (see Isaiah 63:9).
Libnah was a city on the Philistine plain near Lachish. Sennacherib was preparing to fight both Egypt and Jerusalem when he sent word to Hezekiah.
King Tirhakah of Ethiopia was then the ruler of Egypt.

The argument was that Judah’s god, like the gods of other nations already conquered by Assyria, would be unable to save Judah (see also Isaiah 36:18-20). • Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, . . . Eden, and Tel-assar were cities in Mesopotamia.

When he received Sennacherib’s boastful threat, Hezekiah returned to the Temple and prayed for rescue. His prayer stands in contrast to Ahaz’s response to danger decades earlier (see ch Isaiah 7:1-25).

God of Israel: Hezekiah was not taken in by the false claims of Sennacherib that the Lord was powerless. In his prayer, Hezekiah acknowledged that, because the Lord is the Creator, he is God of all the kingdoms of the earth. The Lord is sovereign over all kingdoms. • The mighty cherubim were located in the Temple atop the Ark of the Covenant, which was God’s throne in his Temple (see study note on Lev 16:2; see also Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1).

you alone, O Lord, are God: Hezekiah was concerned for the Lord’s reputation, which Sennacherib had impugned. Hezekiah recognized that if the Lord defeated the Assyrians and their gods, his holy name would be glorified among all the nations of the world (cp. Exodus 9:16; Exodus 14:4, Exodus 14:17-18; Joshua 2:9-11; 1 Sam 4:7-8).
Because you prayed: Prayer is powerful; it moved God’s heart and was part of the reason why the Lord answered with this message of hope.
The virgin daughter of Zion: Jerusalem is personified as a young woman who mocks the Assyrian king (see also Isaiah 3:26).
Whom . . . Against whom: Sennacherib’s speech was not so much an insult against Judah as it was against the Lord.

Isaiah seems to be familiar with the typical royal Assyrian boasts, including that they possessed the highest mountains. These words sound very much like those found in the annals of the Assyrian kings inscribed on the walls of their temples.

I have dug wells . . . I stopped up all the rivers of Egypt: Sennacherib’s boasts demonstrate his attitude of independence. However, the Lord alone is sovereign over nature (Isaiah 42:15; Isaiah 43:19; Isaiah 44:27).

I planned for you to crush . . . into heaps of rubble: Assyria was God’s agent of destruction, but the Assyrians did not realize that they were only a tool in God’s hand (see ch Isaiah 10:1-34), fulfilling what God had planned long before (Isaiah 14:24-27).
you have raged against me: Assyria was utterly hostile to the Lord, which brought them even greater condemnation.
my hook . . . my bit: The Assyrians would be led away like animals, just as they had led so many of their captives away.

This year . . . next year . . . the third year: Because of the Assyrian siege and its destruction of agriculture, the people of Judah would not be able to plant and harvest as usual. The promise that life would resume after the siege assured them that God was with them and would provide as they carried out their everyday activities. They needed to develop their trust in God over a period of three calendar years in the confident expectation that God’s word would be true (cp. Isaiah 30:15, Isaiah 30:18). Perhaps the point was that after rescue from the Assyrians, it would be too late in the present year for fall planting. They would have to wait until fall in the second year to plant again, and they would reap their first crop in the spring and summer of the third year.

In this prophecy of salvation, Isaiah assured Hezekiah that Jerusalem would be spared and that the remnant was under God’s protection. The names of Isaiah and his sons anticipated God’s rescue (see Isaiah 7:1–11:16). The book’s record of God’s presence and rescue provided assurance that the Lord would always have a remnant that he will protect and rescue.
The passionate commitment of God includes his energetic zeal to keep his promise, the best guarantee his people could ever have (see also Isaiah 9:7).
armies . . . arrow . . . shields . . . banks of earth: Despite their advanced military technology and great power, the Assyrians would not succeed against Jerusalem.
for the sake of my servant David: God had promised David a perpetual dynasty (see Isaiah 9:6-7; 2 Sam 7:8-17).

The angel of the Lord was a special heavenly agent through whom God worked on earth. Often his role was to communicate special messages (see Genesis 16:7-14), but sometimes he brought judgment (see 2 Sam 24:16). • killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers: The Lord began to fulfill what he had repeatedly promised—rescue of Jerusalem and judgment of Assyria (see Isaiah 10:16, Isaiah 10:33-34; Isaiah 30:31; Isaiah 31:8).

One day: Sennacherib was probably killed in 681 BC, about twenty years after his withdrawal from Jerusalem. • Esarhaddon was king of Assyria from 680–669 BC. It is ironic that Sennacherib, who mocked the Lord, was killed by his sons in the temple of his god.

About that time (literally in those days): This is a very general time statement. Hezekiah’s illness and subsequent healing probably preceded Jerusalem’s rescue (chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38), even though Isaiah places it afterward. Merodach-baladan’s reign in Babylon (Isaiah 39:1) ended before Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC. The order in the text indicates a connection between these two events (see Isaiah 38:6).

The story of Hezekiah’s healing connects Hezekiah’s extension of life with Jerusalem’s relief from the Assyrians. The events of this story took place before Jerusalem’s rescue from the Assyrians but were placed in a thematic rather than chronological order. One theme is the importance of prayer (see Isaiah 37:14-20; Isaiah 38:2-3). The Lord does listen! Hezekiah had learned the lesson of trust that his father, Ahaz, refused. As a result, Judah and Jerusalem were spared total destruction by the Assyrians. Yet Hezekiah was not the Messiah, the Son of David promised in Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 9:1-7; Isaiah 11:1-16; Isaiah 16:5; Isaiah 32:1, Isaiah 33:17-22. Thus, these accounts of his failure and mortality (chs Isaiah 38:1–39:8) prepare the reader for the revelation of the true Messiah that follows (chs Isaiah 40:1–66:24).

I have always been faithful to you: Hezekiah’s heart was right with the Lord for most of his reign (2 Kgs 18:1-5), although his dependence on Egypt was a time of weakness when he did not act faithfully (Isaiah 31:1-9).
the God of your ancestor David: Hezekiah faithfully walked in David’s footsteps (see Isaiah 37:35; Isaiah 38:1-22).

I will rescue you . . . I will defend this city: This promise refers to the rescue of Jerusalem (chs Isaiah 36:1–37:38); it also provides a greater context for understanding Hezekiah’s sickness and healing. Just as Hezekiah received another fifteen years, Jerusalem also received a temporary reprieve (see ch Isaiah 39:1-8).
Hezekiah’s poem contains both lament (Isaiah 38:9-14) and praise (Isaiah 38:15-20), although the praise is distinctly muted until the final verse.

enter the place of the dead? (literally enter the gates of Sheol?): This image comes from an ancient idea that people enter death through gates (see Isaiah 14:9). Old Testament believers did not understand the afterlife as the New Testament reveals it. It was a shadowy place where all the dead were together and where no praise of God existed (see Isaiah 38:18; Psalm 88:10; Psalm 115:17).
Hezekiah lamented that if he died, he would not enjoy fellowship with God, his family, and his friends.
These images depicted the brevity of life (cp. 2 Cor 5:1).
I will walk humbly: Hezekiah might have previously taken his life and good health for granted. Now he recognized that these gifts from the Lord can be withdrawn at any time.
God’s restoration of Hezekiah’s health also symbolized the restoration from exile that Judah would experience in the future.

Hezekiah received a sign, reminiscent of another sign the prophet had offered Ahaz (Isaiah 7:11). Ahaz and Hezekiah were two bookends to a long story. Ahaz represented the ungodly king and Hezekiah the godly king. The former brought disaster on his people, while the latter rescued his people (but see ch Isaiah 39:1-8).
Hezekiah could not go to the Temple with an infection (see Leviticus 13:1-59), so going to the Temple signifies restored health.

Merodach-baladan, the king of Babylon (722–710 and 704–703 BC), planned to rebel against Assyria and sought help from Hezekiah. His envoys visited after Hezekiah had been very sick and had recovered but before Sennacherib’s final attack in 701 BC.
Hezekiah was exemplary in godliness, prayer, and care for the people of Jerusalem. But he failed the Lord by parading his financial and military strength before the envoys from Babylon.
silver . . . aromatic oils . . . his armory: Showing these treasures demonstrated to Babylon’s envoys that Hezekiah had the resources to be a worthy ally.

carried off to Babylon: This prophecy was given before the prophecy of the rescue of Jerusalem (Isaiah 37:35). Although this pronouncement of judgment and exile comes as a surprise ending to the story of Hezekiah, the exile of both Israel and Judah had been in the background from the beginning (Isaiah 10:3-4, Isaiah 10:20-23). The Lord had promised that he would spare Judah and Jerusalem when the Assyrians attacked in 701 BC, but he had clearly revealed to Isaiah that worse things would come if they did not change their ways. God had demonstrated the truth of his sovereignty and trustworthiness in his defeat of the Assyrians, but that did not mean the people had changed. The only way the promises of Isaiah 2:1-5 and Isaiah 4:2-6 were going to be realized was through the fires of judgment (Isaiah 4:4). Until the burning coal of exile was applied to the nation’s unclean lips (Isaiah 6:5-7), their mission to the nations would fail.

This chapter introduces chs Isaiah 40:1–66:24. In this section, comfort refers to the result of God’s merciful way of dealing with people in the age to come. It includes encouragement, strength, and acceptance. God wants to rescue his people (Isaiah 40:1-11) and is more than able to do so (Isaiah 40:12-26). The exiles needed to believe God’s promises and wait on him for their rescue (Isaiah 40:27-31; see also Isaiah 30:15-18).

This section announces the good news of God’s coming salvation. The Lord is coming to vindicate his own and to judge his enemies. Salvation would be accomplished through the arrival, suffering, and exaltation of the Lord’s servant—the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

The rest of Isaiah provides a message of comfort and a revelation of God’s character and his purposes for Israel. As Isaiah 39:6-7 predicted, Judah would experience judgment and exile after the time of Isaiah. Throughout chs Isaiah 40:1–66:24, Isaiah prophesied from the vantage point of the Exile having already become a reality. Therefore, the Babylonian exile provides the background for understanding these chapters.

Speak tenderly: The prophet’s message was to encourage Jerusalem with the good news of God’s forgiveness, reconciliation, and restoration. • From the prophetic perspective, Israel’s sad days are gone because the Exile is over. • punished her twice over for all her sins: Israel experienced the full brunt of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:19-23; cp. Isaiah 61:7).

the voice of someone shouting: In Malachi 3:1 this person (possibly the Elijah of Malachi 4:5) was God’s messenger who prepared the way for God’s coming. In the Gospels, this announcer was identified with John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4; John 1:23). • Clear the way . . . Make a straight highway: The announcer’s message would expedite God’s coming (see Isaiah 35:8). As God made a way for Israel through the Red Sea (Isaiah 43:16), so a way would be opened up for the Lord (see Isaiah 52:11-12).

There is now a shift from the general announcement of the good news to the specific expectation of God’s coming. The good news (Isaiah 40:1-2) is grounded in God himself. Isaiah portrayed the Lord as coming on a highway through the desert (see ch Isaiah 35:1-10), although the imagery is here reversed: In ch Isaiah 35:1-10, the people were traveling to Zion, toward the Lord. Here, the Lord is coming toward his people (see also Isaiah 52:8, where the two images are brought together).

The future revelation of God’s glory would include the return of Judah from exile but would also go beyond it. The New Testament confirmed that the revelation of God’s glory came in Jesus Christ (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:3). • The Lord has spoken: The coming salvation and judgment would certainly occur because the Lord, who keeps his word, had declared it (see Isaiah 1:20; Isaiah 58:14).
Shout: So that all can hear. • People are not worthy of the revelation of God’s glory because they are mortal.
All humanity is mortal and fleeting. By contrast, God persists in his plans and succeeds. Time does not limit him from carrying out his will (see Isaiah 14:24).
The breath of the Lord refers to God’s spoken words of judgment (see Isaiah 4:4).

the word of our God stands forever: All of God’s words (his plans as well as the written word) will succeed. God might frustrate human expectations, but everything will happen according to his wise plan (see Isaiah 14:24; Isaiah 55:8-11; see also Matthew 25:34).
God is coming to save and restore human beings (see also Isaiah 35:4; Revelation 22:12).
God is the good news. Although he comes like a warrior to rescue his people with power, he also holds them tenderly as a shepherd.

The Lord’s rule is not like that of the unjust and powerless rulers whom he will judge. It is compassionate, just, righteous, and powerful. • with a powerful arm: God manifested his power in events such as the defeat of the Egyptians (Isaiah 63:12), the judgment of his enemies (Isaiah 30:30; Isaiah 48:14; Isaiah 51:9), and the rescue of his people (Isaiah 59:16).

Isaiah used the familiar biblical metaphor of a shepherd to speak of God’s care for his people (see also Isaiah 49:10; Psalm 23:1; Jeremiah 3:15; Jeremiah 23:4; Ezekiel 34:11-17; Matthew 2:6; John 10:1-18).
These rhetorical questions evoke the answer “No one!” God alone created all that exists. He will judge creation (Isaiah 24:17), and he alone can and will restore creation through his salvation.
Against the backdrop of Israel’s questions (spoken by the prophet), the Lord affirmed that he is the incomparable God, a wise and sovereign creator who rules over the nations.

God is sovereign over all the nations of the world and over their human power structures. In comparison to God, they are almost nothing. This included the Babylonian Empire, which was merely a tool in God’s hand. • whole earth: Literally coastlands or islands.
Lebanon was prized for its abundance of wood and its wildlife (see Isaiah 2:13-16; Psalm 104:16-17).

The nations, including their leaders (Isaiah 40:23), pagan structures (Isaiah 41:24, Isaiah 41:29; Isaiah 44:9-11), and all enemies of God’s people (Isaiah 41:11-12), are worth nothing apart from God.

To whom . . . What image: Earlier in the book, idolatry was shown to be ridiculous (Isaiah 16:12; Isaiah 37:16-19). Chapters Isaiah 40:1–48:22 open up a much more extensive argument against idolatry. Idols are symbolic representations of gods and, at times, other religious concepts. Those who worship them don’t recognize the implication that they are man-made trinkets. Idols are powerless (Isaiah 41:7, Isaiah 41:22-24; Isaiah 48:14), give a false sense of security (Isaiah 42:17), delude people (Isaiah 44:20), and lead to severe disappointment (Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 45:16, Isaiah 45:20). They cannot help those who care for them. In fact, they are so weak that they fall down (Isaiah 40:20; Isaiah 41:7). In the end, idols compete for God’s glory (Isaiah 42:8) and take away human dignity (Isaiah 44:9; see also Isaiah 41:21-29). • The Lord, the true God, is incomparable (see Isaiah 40:25; Isaiah 46:5; Psalm 86:8; Psalm 89:6); no one could resemble him.
image that won’t fall down: This is a sarcastic remark; it would be embarrassing if the idol did not even have the power to remain standing (see Isaiah 40:18; Isaiah 41:7; 1 Sam 5:4).

Idolaters fail to discern who God is or to respond wisely to him. The godly in Israel would understand and see the hand of God in the unfolding story of redemption, which includes both exile and restoration (Isaiah 41:20).

God sits enthroned as King over all the earth (see Isaiah 6:1; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1; Psalm 102:12; Psalm 113:5). God is so immense and awesome that humans are like grasshoppers in comparison. • Belief in God as creator of the heavens and earth contradicts the popular Babylonian and Egyptian belief that the sun, moon, and stars represent gods. • like a curtain . . . his tent: See also Psalm 104:2.
great people: God is unimpressed by human power and fame.
The Holy One is a shortened form of “the Holy One of Israel,” a common designation for God in Isaiah (see also Isaiah 10:17; Isaiah 43:15; Psalm 22:3).

Look up into the heavens: Just as God directed Abraham to look into the sky (Genesis 15:5), he also directed Israel to look to the stars for encouragement (see also Isaiah 51:2-3). The cosmos bears witness to God’s great power and incomparable strength. The Strong One is able to strengthen the weak (Isaiah 40:27-31; see Psalm 147:5).

does not see your troubles . . . ignores your rights: The coming exile, a period when God’s powerful presence and rescue would not be seen, would prompt questions (see also Isaiah 49:14; Isaiah 54:7; Lamentations 5:20-22).

heard . . . understood: Cp. Isaiah 40:21. • the everlasting God, the Creator of all the earth: Creation reveals God’s power and wisdom. He is also the Creator of the age to come, a world of righteousness, justice, and peace (Isaiah 45:8; Isaiah 48:6-7; Isaiah 65:17-18). • He never grows weak or weary: God is not susceptible to human limitations.
The weak in this context are those who face persecution or oppression (such as the Babylonian exile); the Lord is their only recourse (see Isaiah 49:4-5; Isaiah 50:4; Psalm 68:9; Psalm 119:28).

trust in the Lord: See Isaiah 33:2; Isaiah 49:23; Isaiah 51:5. • like eagles: This powerful image of rescue reminded readers of the Exodus event of long ago (Exodus 19:4; Deuteronomy 32:10-12; see also Psalm 103:5).

The nations coming together for a trial have to listen in silence to the presentation of God’s arguments. • Bring your strongest arguments: Literally let them find new strength, a play on Isaiah 40:31. • God invited the nations to come . . . and speak, challenging them to refute his case.

The Lord here invited the nations to a trial where he would prove that he alone is God. They were defenseless as he declared that a king from the east (Isaiah 41:2) would crush Babylon, opening the way for Israel to return.

This king from the east was Cyrus, the Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and permitted the Jews to return to their land and rebuild Jerusalem (538 BC; Ezra 1:1-4). Isaiah’s prophecies about Cyrus (see Isaiah 44:28–45:13; Isaiah 48:14-15) encouraged Israel to look to the Lord as sovereign over all of human history, including the actions of great kings. • Who gives this man victory over many nations? As victorious as the conquering Cyrus was, he was still subject to the Lord.

each new generation from the beginning of time: God is sovereign over all things. From the beginning he has unfolded each stage of history according to his plan. • In the book of Revelation, Jesus identifies himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End (Revelation 1:8, Revelation 1:17; Revelation 2:8; Revelation 21:6; Revelation 22:13). • I alone am he: The Lord alone is God (see also Isaiah 43:10, Isaiah 43:13; Isaiah 46:4; Isaiah 48:12; Deuteronomy 32:39). Jesus used similar expressions for himself (see John 6:35; John 8:12, John 8:24; John 9:5; John 10:7, John 10:9, John 10:11, John 10:14; John 11:25; John 14:6; John 15:1, John 15:5).
This taunt against idolatry was a response to God’s raising up of Cyrus; the nations hope to find protection in their idols.
Be strong! The nations put their hope in things that have no strength, objects made by human craftsmen.

The servant—here the nation of Israel—was God’s chosen one, whose calling was grounded in God’s purposes. • Abraham my friend: The phrase in Hebrew could mean Abraham who loves me or Abraham whom I love. See also James 2:23.
These two prophecies of salvation for God’s servant Israel (Isaiah 41:8-13, Isaiah 41:14-16) prepare for the first of the suffering servant songs (see study note on 42:1-4).

I have chosen you restates Isaiah 41:8 to emphasize God’s commitment and faithfulness to his people Israel, who had not been faithful to him. • not throw you away: Because of the Exile, the people felt that God had rejected them (see Isaiah 49:21; Isaiah 54:6). However, God had good purposes for them.

I am with you: The promise of God’s presence (see Isaiah 7:14) is central to the Bible. Because God is present, his people do not need to fear (see also Isaiah 43:1-2, Isaiah 43:5). • I am your God: The Lord used the language of the covenant to affirm that he is their God and that they are his people (see also Jeremiah 7:23; Jeremiah 31:1, Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 14:11; Ezekiel 36:28; Ezekiel 37:27; Zechariah 8:8). • hold you . . . my victorious right hand: The Lord used language reminiscent of the Exodus (cp. Exodus 15:6) to encourage Israel (see also Isaiah 41:13; Isaiah 63:12).

In exile, Israel was in a lowly state. • God is the Redeemer. He works mightily to rescue and restore people from sin and its consequences (for Israel, the Exile; for application to Jesus, see Luke 2:38; Luke 21:28; Romans 3:24; 1 Cor 1:30; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:1-14; Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:12).
When the grain is thrown into the wind, the chaff is blown away. Likewise, Israel’s enemies appeared to be strong but would easily be driven off.

rivers . . . fountains . . . pools of water . . . springs: These images would strike a responsive chord in an agrarian culture. They also suggest that rescue from the Exile would be a second exodus (cp. Exodus 15:27; Exodus 17:6).
the King of Israel: See Isaiah 6:5; Isaiah 43:15; Isaiah 44:6.

This trial scene develops the Lord’s case against idolatry. Idols are nothing but a human creation, whereas God is the Creator of all things. Idols cannot speak, act, accomplish anything, or save their worshipers.

I have stirred up a leader: The God who had planned the Exile through Babylon had already planned for Israel’s restoration from exile through Cyrus (see Isaiah 41:2; see also Isaiah 13:17). • Although Persia is located to the east, rough terrain required those traveling to Israel and Judah to enter from the north. • I will give him victory . . . He will trample them: As Babylon was sent to trample Assyria, so Persia would trample Babylon.
Idols and false gods could not predict the future.
The messenger with good news told of God’s coming to rescue his people (see Isaiah 40:9).

who pleases me: God used similar language at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). • I have put my Spirit upon him: Any leader might be called a servant, but the presence of the Spirit suggests a king of David’s line or a prophet like Moses (see Numbers 11:17, Numbers 11:24-29). • Establishing justice is the responsibility of a king (see Isaiah 9:6-7; Psalm 72:1). • This king’s mission will be a greater mission to the nations than simply governing the small nation of Judah.

The servant here is not the people Israel (as in Isaiah 41:8-28 and elsewhere in chs Isaiah 41:1–48:22; see Isaiah 49:5-6) but is a royal figure who accomplishes his mission with care for people, especially for those who are hurting. The passage is the first of four songs about this servant (Isaiah 42:1-4; Isaiah 49:1-13; Isaiah 50:4-11; Isaiah 52:13–53:12). He brings in an era of universal justice. For the connection of the servant with Jesus Christ, see Matthew 12:18-21.
shout or raise his voice: The royal servant will have calm confidence in his message and calling from God (see also Isaiah 11:1-5).
The royal servant will be gentle with the oppressed and discouraged (see Isaiah 3:15; Isaiah 41:17).

distant lands: The nations long for justice and for instruction on bringing it about. In this regard the servant is like Moses, to whom the law was given. However, the servant is greater in that he extends justice beyond Israel to all the nations.

my people, Israel . . . my covenant with them (literally a covenant for the people): It is also possible that “the people” referred to all the peoples/nations of the earth (see Isaiah 49:6). • light to guide the nations: See also Isaiah 51:4; Acts 13:47.

The servant will open the eyes of the spiritually blind (see Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 29:18) and free the spiritual captives from the prison of sin, in addition to those who were captive in the Babylonian exile (see Isaiah 61:1 with Luke 4:18).
I am the Lord: As Creator of the world, and as the only one who can bring about the things he predicts, the Lord alone is glorious and worthy of praise.

The various geographical regions represent the extremes of human habitation. The whole earth is called to praise God for his commitment to redeem humanity. • Kedar and Sela (Isaiah 42:11; see also Isaiah 16:1; Isaiah 21:16-17) were representative desert sites.

a mighty hero . . . a warrior: The background of this theme is God’s victory at the Red Sea during the Exodus (Exodus 15:3). • God will be victorious over all his enemies in order to rescue his people (Isaiah 51:9; Isaiah 63:1-6; see also Psalm 54:7; Psalm 108:9; Psalm 112:8).

I have long been silent . . . restrained myself: Israel had experienced God’s absence in the Exile, which came about because of their idolatrous ways (Isaiah 57:11-13; 2 Kgs 17:6-24). The godly will pray for God’s presence and renewed involvement in their situation (Isaiah 64:12), and the Lord will answer their prayers because of his commitment to their redemption (Isaiah 62:1, Isaiah 62:6).

The Israelites who refused to listen to what God said and to understand what they saw God doing in history were rendered spiritually blind and deaf (see Isaiah 6:9-10). They had knowledge of the truth through God’s word and the prophets, but their closed minds refused to act upon it.
exalted his glorious law: God’s word is a witness to his righteous rule (see Isaiah 1:10).

Throughout its history, Israel’s sin (Isaiah 42:24) made Israel fair game for foreign oppressors. Many nations, Assyria and Babylon in particular, became instruments God used to pour out his fury (Isaiah 42:25) on his rebellious people.
Generation after generation of Israelites did not learn their lesson, even when God disciplined them through military defeat.

the Lord who created you: The language of creation (see study note on 40:28) was now applied to God’s formation of the nation Israel. • I have ransomed you: At the Exodus, when God brought his people out of bondage. Similarly, God planned to bring his people out of exile and back into their land. Ultimately, Jesus gave his life as a ransom for all humanity (Matthew 20:28; 1 Tim 2:6; Hebrews 9:15) • I have called you by name; you are mine: Despite having faced his wrath, the people of Israel are still God’s chosen people.
In this promise of salvation, the Lord addressed his plundered people in the first person.

Conquering forces could be compared to flooding rivers (see Isaiah 8:8). • I will be with you: God is committed to being with his people to protect and care for them (see Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 41:10; Isaiah 43:5; Isaiah 45:14). • Israel experienced God’s judgment as the fire of oppression during the Exile.
One of God’s purposes in restoring his people was to display his glory to the watching world.

The Lord here called on Israel, his blind servant, to be his star witness in a mock trial against idols and false gods. Israel knew that the Lord alone is God, and the people had experienced his salvation.

you are my witnesses: By their very presence in exile, Israel was evidence that God is truly God. He predicted the Exile long beforehand, and now it had come to pass. God alone is the true God because he speaks and acts and controls all of history. Idols and false gods could do none of these things. Israel would later become even greater evidence because God had also predicted their redemption (Isaiah 43:11-12).
The Lord assured Israel of its coming redemption from Babylon; the redemption would be modeled on Israel’s past redemption from Egypt and would be greater in some ways (Isaiah 43:18).
God did not want the Israelites to forget the exodus from Egypt. However, they needed to look forward in faith to the spectacular event that was about to occur rather than dwelling on the past.
One purpose of redemption is to honor God through the praises of the redeemed (see 1 Pet 2:9).

Israel’s history of rebellion had led them into crisis after crisis, yet their rebellion was so great that they stubbornly refused to ask God for help. When they did pray, their wickedness often caused their prayers not to be heard (Isaiah 1:15).
God alone can and does blot out . . . sins, no matter how many or how great (see also Isaiah 44:22).
leaders: God held Israel’s and Judah’s kings especially responsible for leading the nation into sin (see 2 Kgs 21).

The promise of salvation extended the usefulness of sinful Israel to another generation (Isaiah 44:3). The past was bleak (see Isaiah 43:22-28), but the future would be a glorious new era transformed by the Spirit.

The restoration theme is connected with God’s promise to pour out the Spirit (see also Isaiah 32:15-17; Joel 2:28-32; Acts 2:16-18). • on your descendants . . . children: The next generation of Israelites offered hope.
This passage uses the form of a trial speech to press God’s argument that disgrace comes to all who trust in idols and false gods.

he uses part of the wood to make a fire . . . he takes the rest of it and makes himself a god to worship: This description of the process of making an idol drips with sarcasm and ridicule at the stupidity of the foolish idol worshipers (see also Isaiah 44:19).
