Their minds are shut: Idol worshipers cannot see the irony in using one part of a log to warm themselves and another part of the same log to be their god.
The Lord promised to forgive Israel’s sins.
All creation is called to celebrate God’s redemption of Israel (cp. Isaiah 1:2).
The Lord alone is sovereign over history. He raised up Cyrus of Persia to execute judgment on Babylon and restore Israel to the Holy Land.

False prophets and fortune-tellers used forbidden forms of divination to try to predict the future. Eventually God would expose them as deluded liars (see Isaiah 3:2; Isaiah 9:15; Isaiah 47:13; Deuteronomy 18:10-11).

The sudden depletion of natural resources at times indicates a divine judgment (see Isaiah 42:15; cp. Isaiah 43:20). Here, however, God’s ability to dry up streams with just a word illustrates his power to do what he said he would do through Cyrus of Persia.

He is my shepherd: Cyrus went beyond simply permitting the Jews to return to their homeland. He facilitated a major restoration project to rebuild Jerusalem and restore the Temple (see Isaiah 45:13; Ezra 1:2-4; Ezra 6:3-5).

anointed one: This designation, commonly reserved for David or the Messiah, is here applied to Cyrus. Cyrus was anointed in the sense that he was selected to fulfill a special mission. This title was never used of any other foreign ruler (cp. 1 Sam 10:1; Romans 13:1). • whose right hand he will empower: The Lord would give Cyrus victory over Babylon (see Isaiah 43:14).
so you may know: Cyrus’s victories provided factual proof that the Lord has the power to fulfill his plans, whereas idols and false gods do not (see Isaiah 41:21-29).

I call you by name: Cyrus did not know the Lord, but the Lord knew him. Isaiah predicted the rescuer Cyrus by name 150 years in advance. This prophecy would prove to the exiles that the Lord is indeed God and that he knows the future.
light . . . darkness . . . good times and bad times: Everything is under God’s control.
pot . . . its maker . . . baby . . . its father: It is ridiculous for a creature to question the wisdom of its creator.

The Lord confronts those who question his right to use a pagan king to achieve his purposes. He, the Creator, is free and sovereign in his activities. He promised to bring his people back to their land, and he would use anyone he chose to accomplish that purpose.

Egyptians . . . Ethiopians . . . Sabeans: Israel’s restoration would bring them a new sovereignty. Foreign nations would honor God, and because they recognized God’s special blessing on his people, they would also want to honor his people.
Israel would never again be humiliated and disgraced, oppressed, harassed, or abused. The finality of these declarations suggests that this promise will be fulfilled at the end of time.
Ancient pagan people viewed the world as a place of empty chaos. However, God’s purposes are good, and he made the world from the beginning as a place to be lived in with him in harmony.

Salvation is from the Lord alone. He is the creator, the revealer, and the executor of his will in human history. He promised to establish a new era of salvation and righteousness (see Isaiah 45:8). Every human being will submit to God, either willingly or unwillingly (Isaiah 45:23-24).

Let all the world look to me: All humanity needs to seek the Lord, the true God who created all things, while he may be found (Isaiah 55:6). • In God there is salvation, the only hope for all of humanity (Isaiah 45:8).

God’s words are always true. God’s swearing by his own name reinforces the certainty that he will never go back on his word (see also Isaiah 14:24; Isaiah 54:9; Isaiah 62:8; Hebrews 6:13). • Every knee . . . every tongue: At the end of time all nations will submit to his authority, whether willingly or unwillingly (see Romans 14:11; 1 Cor 15:25-27; Philippians 2:10-11).
In this context, the people are all who turn to the Lord for salvation, even those from foreign nations (Isaiah 45:22).
justified: Literally righteous (see also Isaiah 45:8, Isaiah 45:24).

Marduk-bel was the most important god in the Babylonian pantheon. Bel (similar to “Baal”) designated lordship. • Nebo (Nabu, Nebu), the patron deity of Babylonian scribes, was thought to be the son of Marduk-bel. • Instead of being paraded in glory at a Babylonian festival, these gods would be hauled away on ox carts and disposed of, rejected by the Babylonian people.
This taunt was against the self-contradiction of Babylonian religion.

Those who remain in Israel refers to the remnant that would be left alive after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. • The Lord, the Creator of humanity, cares for and carries his people (contrast the Babylonian idols that must be carried instead). • since you were born . . . before you were born: The Lord chose Israel even before they were a nation (see also Isaiah 49:5).
Many of the exiles would be completely discouraged and not believe the prediction of God’s rescue. God challenged this unbelief.

God knows the future before it even happens; he has comprehensive control over all events, and all his acts match his words (Isaiah 41:4, Isaiah 41:26). He is the First and the Last (Isaiah 44:6; Isaiah 48:12).
The swift bird of prey from the east refers to Cyrus, the Persian king (see study note on 41:2).
Formerly, Israel cared little for doing right (literally righteousness; see also Isaiah 58:2; Isaiah 59:9).

The good news for Israel was that God was coming to set things right (literally I will bring my righteousness near; see Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 51:5). • show my glory to Israel: Unlike a craftsman who bestows material splendor on an idol (Isaiah 44:13), the Lord bestows true dignity on his people.
To sit in the dust was a way of expressing humiliation.
In this taunt against Babylon, the queen of nations is humiliated, forced to work as a servant girl.

Two conclusions can be drawn from the preceding evidence that the Lord alone is God: (1) Babylon’s great pride is foolishness (Isaiah 47:1-15); (2) Israel needs to pay attention to the word of the Lord (Isaiah 48:1-22).
God’s vengeance against those who oppose him and those who oppress his people (see Isaiah 34:8) will bring justice to the world by purging it of wickedness.
Babylon’s confidence and arrogance were well known (see Isaiah 14:13-17; Daniel 4:30). All of this nation’s charms, magic, and wisdom were useless against the disaster decreed for it.
The people of Israel had provoked God’s wrath, prompting him to use Babylon to punish them. Now wicked Babylon itself would be punished.

I am the only one, and there is no other: This was a claim to divinity (cp. Isaiah 45:5; Isaiah 47:10). Only the Lord can make such a claim. For any created thing, including a nation, to utter this is the height of hubris. • To be a widow or to lose one’s children was a disgrace.
Witchcraft and magic were commonly used in an attempt to ward off evil and to secure a happy future.

In this context, ‘wisdom’ and ‘knowledge’ probably refer sarcastically to the pseudo-knowledge gained through occult practices, which actually led Babylon away from the truth and into disaster (Isaiah 47:11).
In the face of calamity, Babylon would turn to occult practices for help, but it would not find help.
Babylon was advanced in astronomy, which the astrologers and stargazers used as a form of divination (see Daniel 2:2, Daniel 2:10; Daniel 5:7).
Jacob . . . Judah: Although Isaiah’s normal focus was on Judah, here he addressed all the tribes of Israel.
Israel was religious but not truly committed to the Lord.
This prophecy is a disputation, a speech in which the prophet argues a set of points against his audience.
The Lord here calls on Israel to forsake her historic rebelliousness and listen to what he says. The Hebrew word translated listening is often synonymous with obeying or acting upon what is heard.
The Lord had forewarned Israel of what was going to happen in the Exile.

Even though Israel had repeatedly failed to believe God’s past predictions, here he revealed new things that were not yet heard. Specifically, God revealed that Babylon would fall and Israel would be restored.
The Exile was a furnace of suffering (cp. Deuteronomy 4:20) through which God refined Israel.

I will not let my reputation be tarnished: Israel’s exile raised questions among the nations about the Lord’s character and reputation. The nations would not have perceived that Israel’s wicked character led to the Exile. Instead they would have viewed it as a failure of Israel’s God to protect his people and their land (see Isaiah 36:19-20; Isaiah 37:12; Ezekiel 36:19-26).
This final trial speech reviews the arguments of chs Isaiah 40:1–48:22 and announces the final conclusion.
chosen Cyrus (literally him) as his ally: See Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1-2.
I will send him and will help him succeed: Cyrus would humiliate Babylon and liberate Israel (Isaiah 45:1-4).

I have told you plainly: God’s promises are clear, though not always specific as to manner and time. • now the Sovereign Lord and his Spirit have sent me with this message: The identity of the one who is sent is unclear. Isaiah might be referring to himself as a Spirit-inspired prophet who spoke the very words of God to Israel. The connection with the Spirit suggests that it refers to the promised servant, the Messiah. • The presence of the Spirit assures the servant’s success.

Peace and righteousness will be established when the Kingdom of God comes in its fullness (see Isaiah 66:12). • like a gentle river . . . like waves: An abundance of comforting peace and overflowing resources of righteousness (cp. Amos 5:24) could have been Israel’s if its people had only listened to God.
Your descendants . . . like the sands: This would fulfill God’s covenant to Abraham (Genesis 22:17); by contrast, the Israelites were nearly wiped out in the Exile (see Isaiah 44:26).
Leave Babylon: See also Isaiah 52:11-12; Isaiah 55:12.

not thirsty . . . rock . . . water gushed: These reminders of God’s provision in the Exodus provide a fitting summary of what he would do to rescue Israel from captivity in Babylon (see Numbers 20:11).

This refrain, no peace for the wicked (also Isaiah 57:21), continues the sharp divide between the godly and the wicked (see Isaiah 66:24). Peace speaks of God’s kingdom, from which the wicked are excluded.

distant lands: The servant’s ministry would extend beyond Israel (see Isaiah 42:4, Isaiah 42:10, Isaiah 42:12; Isaiah 51:5; Isaiah 60:9; Isaiah 66:19). • called me before my birth . . . from within the womb . . . by name: The promised servant’s prophetic call was similar to the call of Jeremiah (see Jeremiah 1:5; see also Galatians 1:15). It was not a general call but a very specific, personal one (see also Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 45:3-4).

This has traditionally been regarded as the second of four suffering servant songs (see study note on 42:1-4). The suffering role of the promised servant becomes increasingly clear (see also Isaiah 50:4-9; Isaiah 52:13–53:12).

God intended to rescue the Israelites from exile. However, the question remained: How could sinful Israel again become the servant of the Holy One? God would make a way for Israel’s sin to be atoned for and their fellowship with him to be restored. That way would be the promised servant, who would come for Israel and for all peoples. This servant was introduced in Isaiah 42:1-9, but in this passage he becomes the central focus.
my words of judgment: The servant’s mission would be prophetic (see Isaiah 11:4; Ephesians 6:17; Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 1:16; Revelation 2:12, Revelation 2:16; Revelation 19:15).

The suffering servant would come out of Israel (see Isaiah 41:8) and would himself be the true Israel. He would serve as both king (Isaiah 42:1) and prophet (Isaiah 49:1), anointed with the Spirit of God (Isaiah 61:1) and commissioned (Isaiah 48:16) as a faithful witness to God’s purposes (Isaiah 43:12; Isaiah 48:20). In his mission toward both Israel and the other nations (Isaiah 49:6), he would suffer rejection and disgrace while being faithful, unlike the nation of Israel (see Isaiah 50:4-9). His suffering would be on behalf of God’s chosen people. Jesus became the ultimate fulfillment of the suffering servant (see study note on 52:13–53:12).

my work seems so useless . . . to no purpose: Even though people stubbornly refuse his message, the servant would reach out to them. • I will trust God: Despite discouragement and suffering, the servant would continue to discharge his duty faithfully, trusting God for the outcome. God promised to reward the servant’s faithfulness (see also Isaiah 40:10; Isaiah 50:8).

a light to the Gentiles: As the Messiah, the servant’s mission would have a worldwide reach (see Isaiah 11:10, Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 42:6). The apostle Paul explained his apostolic mission to the Gentiles on the basis of this prophecy (Acts 13:47; Acts 26:23).

The promised servant would be despised and rejected by the nations (see Isaiah 52:14–53:5) as well as by his own people (see also Isaiah 50:6-7; Isaiah 53:8-9). • Kings and princes will also bow low to express respect and humility before the servant (see also Isaiah 52:15), whom God will exalt after he has suffered. God is faithful to his servant.

God acts at just the right time to accomplish his purposes (Acts 1:7; 2 Cor 6:2). Israel returned to reestablish the land of Israel after the Exile. The land was restored and the city rebuilt beginning with Cyrus’s edict (Isaiah 44:26-28).

Like a shepherd, the Lord in his mercy will lead the returning exiles beside cool waters; he promised to comfort them and tend to their needs (see also Isaiah 40:11; Psalm 23:1). • level paths . . . highways: The Lord would open up the way of salvation.
The remnant would come from the north (i.e., from Babylon and Persia), from the west by sea, and from as far south as Egypt.
This hymn of praise is in response to the salvation that the servant would make possible.

Although the prophet announced cause for rejoicing (Isaiah 49:8-13), the exiles continued to ponder the calamity that came upon them when Babylon invaded the land, destroyed Jerusalem, and carried the people of Judah into exile where they felt deserted and forgotten.
like jewels or bridal ornaments: As a wedding calls for festivity and public display, so God’s restoration of Israel would be an open act for all to see (see also Isaiah 61:10).

The population explosion would reach beyond Israel to include the members of foreign nations who turn to the Lord (see Isaiah 56:6-8; Revelation 7:9). • more room: The expanded population would require space far beyond the traditional boundaries of the land of Israel (see also Zechariah 2:4).

carry your little sons . . . your daughters: The mighty rulers of the nations, some of whom had previously killed children in Israel, would aid in their return to Zion (see also Isaiah 60:3-9). Elsewhere Isaiah envisioned people of foreign nations streaming to Zion to worship the Lord (see Isaiah 2:2-4).

you will know that I am the Lord: The stunning role-reversal—kings and queens serving the lowly exiles upon their return—would reveal God’s power to do the unimaginable (see also Isaiah 60:16). • The godly would experience temporary disgrace in the Exile but would not ultimately be put to shame, as the idolaters and ungodly were.
Who can snatch . . . Who can demand: The people considered it nearly impossible that they would be rescued from their oppressors.
The Lord is like a warrior who will fight to protect his children, as promised to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; see also Isaiah 54:15).

God was not at fault for the people’s problems; it was their sin that brought about their exile (see also Isaiah 59:1-15). • Jerusalem—the mother city of Judah (Psalm 87:5-6)—was destroyed, and the people of Judah were taken into exile in 586 BC.
This disputation shows that God was not forced to give Israel up, and therefore he could take the nation back as his people if he desired.

Why didn’t anyone answer: The people had not responded to God’s repeated call to trust in him and repent of their sins. They were deaf and stubborn (see Isaiah 6:9-10; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 42:18-19). • The Lord came and called the people through the prophets (see also Isaiah 65:1-3). • Is it because I have no power to rescue? God was fully able to rescue Israel and Judah from the Assyrians and Babylonians, but he first had to deal justly with his people’s sinfulness (see Isaiah 59:1). • speak to the sea and make it dry: This was an allusion to the parting of the Red Sea during the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 14:21-22).

Phenomena such as darkness and the wearing of clothes of mourning were associated with the day of the Lord (Isaiah 13:10; see study note on 2:5-22). The mention of darkness might allude to the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exodus 10:21).
The Lord, who never grows weary (Isaiah 40:28), sends the servant with good news (see Isaiah 40:28-31) to comfort those who are weary (see study note on 40:1-31).
This is the third of four servant songs (see study note on 42:1-4). The faithful and suffering servant portrays an ideal Israel; the image was realized in Jesus Christ.

beat me . . . pulled out my beard . . . mockery and spitting: These connections with the experience of Jesus at his crucifixion are too close to be coincidental—Jesus is the true suffering servant (see Matthew 27:27-31).

Externally, the servant would be disgraced and put to shame, but within himself he would calmly await God’s vindication (see Isaiah 29:22; Isaiah 54:4; Isaiah 61:7). • set my face like a stone: The servant would be determined to do God’s will (see Luke 9:51).

He who gives me justice is near: God vindicates those who suffer for doing his will. Vindication is an act of God by which he exalts those who have been wrongly disgraced and strikes down the wicked, self-exalted, and arrogant (see also 2 Thes 1:6-9). • bring charges . . . my accusers: Confidence in God’s vindication removes fear and bolsters faith (see Romans 8:31-34).
Who will declare me guilty? The implied answer to this rhetorical question is, “No one!” This answer foreshadows the New Testament understanding of justification (see Romans 8:31-35).

The test of whether or not an individual fears the Lord is how he or she responds to God’s righteous servant. The same idea is present in Jesus’ claim that no one can come to the Father except through him (John 14:6). • Those who trust in the Lord have great hope for the future (see Isaiah 12:2).
This is a call for response to the servant’s ministry.
warm yourselves by your own fires: Spiritually complacent people are unresponsive toward God. Though they have comfort and security now, they will soon fall down in great torment (see Isaiah 66:24).
The rock and the quarry represent Abraham and Sarah (Isaiah 51:2).
This prophecy calls for trust in the Lord. Each of its three units begins with the phrase, Listen to me (Isaiah 51:1, Isaiah 51:4, Isaiah 51:7).
Abraham . . . became a great nation: The exiled community had decreased in number. They needed to have faith that God could restore them again to a healthy and thriving population.
Eden . . . the garden of the Lord: God’s salvation will one day reestablish conditions like those in which human beings first lived (see Genesis 2:1–3:24).

my law . . . my justice: The work of the servant will prosper because justice will be the rule in God’s kingdom on earth (see Isaiah 42:1-4). • a light to the nations: The nations will receive the Lord and his revelation (see also Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 60:1-3; Isaiah 66:19-23; Matthew 4:15-16; Luke 2:32; John 1:4-9; John 12:35-50; Acts 13:47).
God is strong enough to crush his enemies and rescue his people, such as when he rescued Israel in the Exodus (see Isaiah 51:9; Exodus 6:6; Exodus 15:16).
die like flies: The wicked will die in great multitudes on the day of God’s judgment.

cherish my law in your hearts: Beyond simply knowing God’s word, the Lord desires for his people to internalize, treasure, and obey it (see also Psalm 37:31; Jeremiah 31:33). • Those who obey the Lord often endure scorn and insults (see also Matthew 5:10-12).

Wake up, wake up: God does not sleep; this prayer is for God to act immediately to save his people (see Isaiah 52:1; see especially God’s military garb in Isaiah 59:17). • in the days of old: The exodus from Egypt was an act of redemption that displayed God’s power as he made a path of escape (Isaiah 51:10) for his people (see also Isaiah 11:15).
you have forgotten the Lord: The Lord will never forget Israel (see Isaiah 44:21; Isaiah 49:15), so they should not forget him. • The Creator of the world also created the nation Israel.
The Exile brought such brutal conditions as imprisonment, starvation, and death.
I am the Lord: The Lord uses this formula to identify himself as the covenant God and to assure his people of the truth of his word and the reliability of his actions (see Isaiah 27:3-4).
my words in your mouth: The focus shifted back to the servant. • You are my people: Israel was the covenant community.

Wake up, wake up: Israel used these words in a prayer to the Lord (Isaiah 51:9). Israel’s problems were not the result of God’s slowness to act; rather, the people were slow to believe God’s promises. • the cup of the Lord’s fury: The Lord will appropriately measure out his judgment; those who fall under his judgment must figuratively drink from his wrath (see also Matthew 26:39).
The prophet called the people of Israel to be done with their past and to anticipate God’s future for them.
children have fainted: A sad commentary on Jerusalem’s desolation is provided in Lamentations 1:13, Lamentations 1:22; Lamentations 2:11-12, Lamentations 2:19.
God would be the Defender of Israel as he was when Assyria besieged Jerusalem (Isaiah 38:6).
The tormentors were the Babylonians who brought about destruction, war, and famine (Isaiah 51:19).

This second call to wake up (see Isaiah 51:17) was in preparation for a glorious future. • holy city: The new city would be holy because its citizens would be holy (see Isaiah 4:3). • enter your gates no longer: Things that are unclean will not be permitted to enter the holy city (see Revelation 21:27).

I sold you into exile . . . Now I can redeem you: The Lord was fully in control when he gave his people into the hands of their enemies. Likewise, he remained fully in control and could redeem them if he chose to do so.
in Egypt . . . oppressed by Assyria: The exodus from exile would be like Israel’s past exodus from Egypt.

The oppressors would shout in exultation because they believed they had conquered not only Israel but also its God. • My name is blasphemed all day long: The condition of God’s people affects God’s reputation in the eyes of the watching world (see Isaiah 37:6, Isaiah 37:23; Isaiah 48:11).
Just as God did to Moses before the Exodus (Exodus 3:15), he will reveal himself in the coming rescue from exile.

How beautiful on the mountains: See Nahum 1:15; Romans 10:15. • The good news goes beyond proclaiming an end to the Exile; it also points to the peace and salvation of the age to come (Isaiah 54:13-14; see Isaiah 40:9-10; Isaiah 41:27).

This is a poetic description of God’s promise to rescue his people from the alienation their sin created. The imagery is of a besieged city waiting for word that its hero has defeated the enemy armies. Paul applies these words to the proclamation of the Good News of the Lord Jesus (Romans 10:15).
The watchmen were those looking for the news of Zion’s redemption. • the Lord returning to Jerusalem: The sin of the city’s inhabitants had driven God away.

victory of our God: The rescue of God’s people from disgrace foreshadows an even greater victory when God will reign victoriously to the ends of the earth (note the many similarities with Psalm 98:1-3).
Here the imagery of leaving the unclean enemy city encourages the people to purify themselves by turning away from all known sin. Those who carry home the sacred objects of the Lord need to be pure.
This is an exhortation to leave the captivity of sin (see Isaiah 48:20 on leaving physical captivity in Babylon). See also 2 Cor 6:17; 2 Tim 2:19.

not leave in a hurry: At the time of the Exodus the people had to leave quickly (see Exodus 12:11, Exodus 12:31-36). Isaiah drew this contrast to emphasize the newness of God’s plan. • protect you from behind: See Exodus 13:21; Exodus 14:19-20.
prosper . . . be highly exalted: The servant would be wise and successful, set apart with the great and noble. Similar terms describe God in Isaiah 6:1 and Isaiah 57:15.

This is the fourth of four passages that speak about the promised servant (see study note on 42:1-4). The Hebrew poem is carefully constructed in five three-line stanzas. It begins with the servant’s exaltation (Isaiah 52:13), proceeds to his humiliation (Isaiah 52:14–53:9), and ends with his exaltation (Isaiah 53:10-12). The faithful servant’s suffering would bring reconciliation between God and humans. The Lord Jesus perfectly fulfilled this prophecy (see ch Isaiah 40:1-31; Matthew 8:17; Acts 8:30-35; Romans 10:15-17; Romans 15:21; 1 Pet 2:24-25).
were amazed: No one expected that the rescuer would suffer and die.
Despite the servant’s greatness, the actual way he would appear on earth would shock people.

startle many nations: They would be amazed that a rescuer would appear so weak and helpless and would stand speechless. • What they will see and what they will understand will be in complete contrast to anything they had previously imagined.

our message: The identity of the speaker has been debated—the main possibilities are (1) a faithful remnant of Israel, and (2) Isaiah himself. Most likely, Isaiah the prophet was speaking for and with Israel. • powerful arm: God’s strength, so dramatically described in the previous chapters (see Isaiah 50:2; Isaiah 51:5, Isaiah 51:9; Isaiah 52:10), would actually manifest itself in weakness and apparent helplessness through the servant’s humiliation and exaltation (see 1 Cor 1:27-30).

a tender green shoot . . . in dry ground: Such a plant is vulnerable to extinction (cp. Isaiah 37:27). It can hardly stay alive for itself, let alone provide anything for anyone else. • nothing beautiful or majestic: The servant appeared to have no greatness or self-evident royal splendor (see Isaiah 52:13-15). • nothing to attract us to him: People like their leaders to be physically attractive and personally charismatic. The servant would be neither.

a man of sorrows, acquainted with deepest grief (or a man of pains, acquainted with illness): The servant would fully experience the effects of sin and the Fall. • we did not care: Because people would fail to see how such a weak, insignificant person could do anything beneficial for them, they would be unconcerned about his suffering.

The callous world would assume that the servant somehow brought his suffering on himself, never realizing that he was suffering for them. • troubles . . . punishment: These descriptions of the servant’s humiliation contrast with the descriptions of his exaltation.

he was pierced: See also Zechariah 12:10. • crushed . . . beaten . . . whipped: These were typically punishments for crimes. Sin is a crime against God. • be whole: Hebrew shalom, usually translated “peace.” Shalom means to experience wholeness in body, in mind, and in relationships with others. The servant would be injured so that humanity can be whole and healthy in all aspects of life (see also Isaiah 57:18). We do not need to suffer divine condemnation for our sins because the servant has already done so (see Galatians 1:4).
strayed away . . . left God’s paths: These are metaphors for sin (see also Romans 3:10-18).
See 1 Pet 2:21-25 for the fulfillment of this prophecy in Jesus Christ.
The Ethiopian eunuch was reading this passage when Philip met him (Acts 8:32-33).
Unjustly condemned: The servant will be given no legal protection or proper defense. • cut short in midstream: To die in midlife was understood to be God’s judgment.

no wrong . . . never deceived anyone: See 1 Pet 2:21-25. • in a rich man’s grave: Literally he was with the rich in his death (see Matthew 27:57-61). Although the Bible often considers riches as a blessing from God, it regularly condemns the rich as crooked and oppressive. The point here might be ironic: This good man would be buried with oppressors.

The servant’s grief would accomplish a greater good; the forgiveness and reconciliation of sinful humanity. Note also God’s good plan to prosper and exalt the servant. • when his life is made an offering for sin: The suffering of the servant provided a substitute for others, just as the animal sacrifices in the Temple did. • Having many descendants and enjoying a long life are rewards for godly and wise living (see Proverbs 3:2; Proverbs 17:6; Proverbs 20:7). Because the servant left his fate in his God’s hands, he would receive eternal rewards from the God who vindicates the righteous (see Philippians 2:9-11).
The final stanza of the poem first explains why the servant suffered and was treated unjustly in the place of others; it then explains what the result of that obedience would be.

his experience (literally his knowledge): This clearly does not refer to intellectual knowledge but to all that the servant would experience in his obedience, suffering, and intimate relationship with God. • The servant’s righteous obedience enables people to be put right with God (see Genesis 15:6; Romans 5:18-19), for he will bear all their sins.

the honors: See Philippians 2:9-11. • He was counted among the rebels: Rebels (Hebrew poshe‘im) is a stronger word than sinners and is a key word in Isaiah. It refers to those who are in willful defiance of a lawful authority, in this case, God. • interceded for rebels: The servant would pray for sinners in the midst of his suffering (see Exodus 32:30; Luke 23:34).

In the ancient world, a woman who had never given birth after being married for a time would be ashamed. Isaiah compares Jerusalem to a barren woman who rejoices at the long-awaited blessing of children (see Galatians 4:27).
The prophet encourages Jerusalem, likened to a barren woman, to rejoice because its fate was rapidly changing. She would have so many children that she would outgrow her home (see Galatians 4:27).

Salvation flows from the vindication of the suffering servant. The promises mentioned here go beyond the return from Babylonian exile and apply to the coming of Jesus Christ, the extension of the kingdom to the church, the benefits of the second coming of Jesus Christ as the bridegroom of the church, and the new Jerusalem.
This is an invitation to participate in the restoration to God’s favor made possible through the ministry of the promised servant.

Israel’s descendants (cp. Isaiah 53:10) would occupy other nations in fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17) and to Jacob (Genesis 28:14). • As desolation took place (Isaiah 6:11; Isaiah 14:21), the people of God would inherit the earth and resettle the ruined cities (Isaiah 51:6; Isaiah 52:10; Isaiah 65:17; see also Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13).

Creator . . . husband: The Lord committed himself to the abandoned woman (his people in exile) as her maker (Isaiah 44:24) and husband (see also Isaiah 62:4-5; Hosea 2:19-20). • The Redeemer transforms misery into freedom and fulfillment (see also Isaiah 41:14).

The pain of separation would be brief compared to the depth of the renewal of love and compassion. • The Lord abandoned Israel in exile for a little while because of the people’s sins. • everlasting love: The Lord is eternally committed to his people, making the seventy-year punishment of exile seem short indeed (see Isaiah 25:1; Hosea 2:1).

The Exile was similar in both drama and trauma to the flood in the time of Noah. In both instances, people sinned grievously against the Lord, but the Lord renewed his commitment to creation (after Noah’s flood) and to his people (after the Exile).

God’s faithful love for his people endures despite their unfaithfulness. • God’s covenant of blessing was the assurance of his presence, resulting in wholeness, blessing, and protection. It replaces the shame and disgrace of the Exile (see Ezekiel 34:25; Ezekiel 37:26).
The Lord himself would rebuild the city (see Hebrews 11:10). • Lapis lazuli is a semi-precious stone.

This is a vision of the renewed Jerusalem as a city under God’s protection, a place of peace and righteousness (see Isaiah 59:21–60:22). This section forms the background of John’s vision of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:10-21).
I will teach: Jesus alluded to this verse in John 6:45. • They will enjoy great peace, the benefits of God’s presence and protection (Isaiah 53:5; see Isaiah 48:17-18; Isaiah 54:10).
Jerusalem would again be a righteous city, secure under a government that is just and fair (see Isaiah 1:26).
God gives assurance that no nation can defeat his people . The Lord has promised to protect them, just as he had promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3; see Isaiah 49:25).

no weapon . . . will succeed . . . accuse you . . . vindication: God will protect his people in war and in the courtroom. • These benefits are enjoyed by the servants of the Lord: Only the true children of God—people who come out of Israel and the nations—will enjoy the promised blessings of the age to come that God establishes.

thirsty . . . wine or milk: The invitation to eat and drink is similar to Wisdom’s call in Proverbs 9:5. The image promises the slaking of thirst not only by water but also by more costly items such as wine and milk. John applied a similar theme to Jesus Christ (John 4:14; John 6:27, John 6:35; John 7:37; Revelation 21:6; Revelation 22:17). • it’s all free: Reconciliation with God is for anyone and has no cost.
This final chapter of the prophecies of comfort (chs Isaiah 40:1–55:13) summarizes the section’s prominent themes: blessing, covenant, witness, word, nations, glory, forgiveness, and joy.
Listen to me . . . eat what is good: Responding positively to God satisfies one’s spiritual, social, and physical being (see Isaiah 1:19; Isaiah 58:13-14; Proverbs 4:10).

Come to me. . . . Listen . . . find life: Those who respond obediently to God’s word find eternal life (see also Isaiah 55:11). • an everlasting covenant . . . I promised to David: King David received a special covenant from God, a promise to preserve his kingly line (see 2 Sam 7:15-16). David’s dynasty was eternally confirmed in the kingship of the Messiah, Jesus Christ (see Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 11:1-16; Acts 2:22-36; Acts 13:34).

while you can find him: When God graciously extends an invitation to salvation, people must respond (Isaiah 65:1; Jeremiah 29:13-14; Hosea 5:6; Hosea 10:12). Those who do not seek him at such times risk never having the opportunity again.
The prophet calls for a response while the time is right.

Let the wicked change . . . turn to the Lord: True conversion demands a change of how we live in favor of God’s requirements (see Isaiah 1:16-17; Isaiah 30:15; Isaiah 59:20). • have mercy on them: God’s compassion reaches out to the needy and finds them where they are. • he will forgive generously: Forgiveness of sin is foundational to the good news of redemption (see Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:14; see also Psalm 32:1; Psalm 86:5; Psalm 99:8; Psalm 103:2-5).

My thoughts are nothing like your thoughts: God’s plans are marvelous (Psalm 92:5; cp. Psalm 94:11). God’s creatures, including humans, can never fully understand the Creator’s thoughts, but his revelation through his messengers gives great insight and knowledge of some of the things he will do.

The Creator not only sends rain and snow but also his word (Hebrew dabar). In this context, dabar means his will or plan (see Isaiah 14:24; Isaiah 40:8). God’s written word, as an expression of God’s plan, accomplishes his purposes. God is effective in whatever he does (see Isaiah 14:26-27; Isaiah 46:10).

Joy is found in being redeemed from bondage. • Godly people experience an inner peace not known to the wicked (Isaiah 48:22). • mountains and hills . . . trees of the field: Creation participates in the freedom of the children of God (Isaiah 44:23; Isaiah 49:11, Isaiah 49:13; see Romans 8:19-23).
The prophet encourages his people to forget the past, to leave Babylon, and to accept the perspective of the coming age.

Redemption is like the transformation from desert to forest (see also Isaiah 35:1; Isaiah 41:19; Isaiah 60:13). • great honor to the Lord’s name: God’s glory will be more and more visible to humanity as his redemption takes effect.

Be just and fair: A key aspect of the message of chs Isaiah 1:1–39:8 is the call for justice in relationship with others and God. True godliness comes only through having character that is shaped by the character of God, which only happens by understanding and consistently applying God’s word. • I am coming soon: This statement summarizes the message of chs Isaiah 40:1–55:13, that the Lord is creating a world of harmony, peace, restoration, vindication, and the removal of enemies (Isaiah 46:13).
This section summarizes chs Isaiah 1:1–55:13 with an invitation to the outcasts to participate in God’s redemption.

This last major division of the book of Isaiah brings together themes from chs Isaiah 1:1–39:8 (sin, justice and righteousness, responsibility, vengeance and vindication) and chs Isaiah 40:1–55:13 (salvation, the age to come).

Blessed: Cp. Isaiah 30:18; Isaiah 32:20; see also Psalm 1:1; Psalm 119:1; Matthew 5:3. • The Sabbath, as a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:13-17), is God’s gift to his people; it belongs to this age as well as to the age to come (Isaiah 56:4, Isaiah 56:6; Isaiah 58:13-14; see Hebrews 4:1-13).

Foreigners who commit themselves to the Lord would become full participants in the covenant community. Previously, their participation had been carefully regulated (Deuteronomy 23:3, Deuteronomy 23:7-8). • eunuchs: In the past, an emasculated person was excluded from the community (Deuteronomy 23:1). Both eunuchs and foreigners had no share in Israel’s holiness and were considered marginal to God’s kingdom. In the age to come, God would bring to the center those who had previously been marginalized (cp. Matthew 20:16).
The blessing (Isaiah 56:2) would extend to eunuchs and to the Gentiles.
The Sabbath is a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:13-17).

within the walls of my house: Those previously excluded would have a place in God’s presence. • a memorial and a name: Everlasting existence in God’s presence is better than the blessing of physical descendants.

The essential ingredient for covenant fellowship is love for God (Deuteronomy 6:5; Deuteronomy 30:20; Matthew 22:34-38). • Keeping the Sabbath is a sign of keeping the covenant itself (see Exodus 31:13-17).

burnt offerings and sacrifices: God had previously rejected sinful Israel’s expressions of piety (Isaiah 1:11-13) but would welcome offerings from righteous Gentiles or foreigners. Nationality is worth little without true piety. • a house of prayer for all nations: The Lord would open the doors of the Temple to all nations (see Isaiah 2:2-4). Jesus rebuked the people for desecrating the Temple and for preventing it from functioning as the house of prayer (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17).

The outcasts of Israel were those dispersed among the nations as the result of the Exile (see also Isaiah 11:12). • The others would be eunuchs and Gentiles (Isaiah 56:3-7; see also Isaiah 57:19; John 10:16).
Wild animals are here a metaphor for the hostile nations surrounding Judah.
This is a reflection on the prevalence of evil among God’s people; they were greedy (Isaiah 56:9-12), hostile to the righteous (Isaiah 57:1-2), and idolatrous (Isaiah 57:3-13).
The leaders of Israel failed to guide and protect God’s people from the sins that led to the Exile. • sleeping and dreaming: See Isaiah 29:10.

ignorant shepherds: Israel’s leaders did not know how to rule in a godly way (see also Ezekiel 34:1-6). By contrast, the Lord is the faithful Shepherd of his people (Isaiah 40:11). • all following their own path: They had no concern for God or his standards of godly leadership (see also Isaiah 53:6). • personal gain: Cp. Isaiah 33:15.
the evil to come: Judgment that would come on the wicked nations. • protecting them: At times, God allows the godly to die in order to protect them from harsher times to come.
This is a lament for the righteous who suffer in a wicked society.
The wicked would not be able to rest in peace (Isaiah 57:21).
witches’ children . . . adulterers and prostitutes: Baal religion, which flourished in Israel before the Exile (see Isaiah 1:21-23), included lewd sexual practices.
mock . . . sticking out your tongues: The wicked oppressed the righteous by their insults (Isaiah 57:1-2; see also Isaiah 28:9, Isaiah 28:14).

beneath the oaks and under every green tree: Tree groves were commonly used as places of pagan worship (see Isaiah 1:29-30). • sacrifice your children: The horrible practice of child sacrifice was occasionally practiced in Israel (see Psalm 106:37-38).
Liquid offerings and grain offerings were believed to satisfy the basic needs of the gods and thus to earn their favor.
climbed into bed: The people of Israel had a sickening commitment to the fertility religions, which included sex as part of their rituals.
The people were living in fear of false gods instead of fearing the Lord (see Isaiah 8:12-13).
The Lord did not consider the people’s so-called good deeds (literally righteousness; see Isaiah 59:16) to be truly righteous.

your idols . . . fall over: See study note on 40:18. • inherit the land: The Hebrew word translated land can also signify the whole earth (see Psalm 25:13; Psalm 37:9, Psalm 37:11, Psalm 37:22, Psalm 37:29, Psalm 37:34; Matthew 5:5). • my holy mountain: God’s servants will enjoy God’s presence in Zion (see Isaiah 2:2; Isaiah 56:7).

The Lord here promises to be present with the humble, to heal them, and to grant them his peace. The promise extends to all the citizens of Zion, both Jews and Gentiles. The Holy One comes to the humble with an all-inclusive offer of salvation, while dealing justly with the wicked.
Even though God is the high and lofty one, he promises to dwell with the humble.
I will heal them anyway: Salvation is by God’s grace (see Isaiah 19:22; Isaiah 30:26; Isaiah 53:5).
words of praise: God’s redemption should bring a response of praise from its recipients. • both near and far: Both Gentiles and Jews are included (see Isaiah 56:3; John 10:16; Ephesians 2:17).

restless sea . . . never still: Those who live in constant opposition to God (see Psalm 46:3, Psalm 46:6; Psalm 93:3-4) do not enjoy inner quiet because they are not at peace with God (Isaiah 30:15; Isaiah 32:17). • churns up mud and dirt: Their activity has little productivity (see Psalm 40:2).
no peace: Cp. Isaiah 57:2; see also Isaiah 48:22.
This is a charge against religious Israelites who were pleased with themselves because of their religious activities.
they act so pious (literally they seek me): They may have been truly committed to a religious form, but they failed to truly meet God in their religious activities.

Fasting should be a time of self-deprivation in order to focus on God and pleasing him (Leviticus 16:29; see Zechariah 7:5). However, these people were only interested in pleasing themselves and continuing in their sins.

This is a satirical portrayal of the people’s fasting as mere external piety without repentance and righteous acts. Ritualistic and insincere fasting is nothing but pomp. • Wearing burlap and ashes are expressions of sorrow and mourning. • please the Lord? The people erroneously believed that the Lord would bless them, if only they performed the right rituals.
True fasting creates an awareness of injustice and oppression and prompts the practitioner to reach out to help the needy in their struggles (see Isaiah 42:7; Matthew 25:35-36; James 1:27).

your salvation (literally your light): The light of the coming age (see Isaiah 42:6-7; Isaiah 60:1-3) will dawn on those who turn fully to the Lord. The night of divine judgment and oppression will be over. • your wounds: The nation of Israel was wounded when they were conquered and sent into exile. • protect you from behind: See also Isaiah 52:12.
the Lord will answer: Cp. Isaiah 1:15; see also Isaiah 19:22. • Stop . . . spreading vicious rumors: God calls for an end to acts and words that destroy relationships (see Proverbs 6:12-14).
your light . . . as bright as noon: God would rescue and vindicate his people (see Job 11:17; Psalm 37:6).
a rebuilder of walls: Nehemiah would later fulfill this promise (see Nehemiah 2:17).

Like the practice of fasting, the Sabbath was intended to be an expression of self-denial and worship. It consists of delighting in the Lord, trusting him to provide for one’s needs while abstaining from work, and living in obedience to his will.

As people honor God through obedience, they themselves will be honored by God. • the inheritance I promised to your ancestor Jacob: The promised inheritance includes living with many descendants in the holy land and enjoying God’s presence, blessing, and protection (Genesis 31:3; Genesis 35:9-12).
not too weak: The delay in their rescue could not be attributed to an inherent weakness in the Lord.
The people complained that the Lord could not rescue them, but the real problem was that they had not repented (Isaiah 59:20) and were still living in sin.
The Lord alone can and will usher in his salvation. Like a warrior, he will break into the world to avenge himself on his enemies and to vindicate his holy people.
your sins . . . cut you off: The Israelites, like all people (Romans 3:15-17), had sinned, which resulted in alienation from God (he has turned away).
being fair and honest: Israel did not practice these qualities that are part of God’s nature and that he expects from people (Isaiah 1:21; see Isaiah 25:1).
The images of deadly snakes and spiders’ webs represent plans designed to destroy others’ lives and relationships.

Paul quotes from these verses in his description of the depravity of all people (Romans 3:15-17). • Misery and destruction: The people lamented being victims of oppression (Isaiah 51:19), yet they were oppressors themselves.
Israel’s history of rebellion was well established. The prophet here confesses the nation’s sins and laments that they could not apprehend the light of God’s salvation.
people without eyes: See Isaiah 6:10; Deuteronomy 28:29.
The people growl and moan with longing for redemption, finally coming to terms with their sinfulness.
The Lord goes out as a warrior intent on achieving victory against the wicked (cp. Ephesians 6:14).
repay his enemies: The Lord will dole out righteous retribution on the whole earth. His justice requires people to be judged for the evil they have done (see also Isaiah 3:9-11; Isaiah 13:9).
In the west . . . in the east: I.e., in all parts of the world.

The members of the new community have the Spirit, and they know and practice God’s word (see also Ezekiel 36:24-28). The Lord promises to regenerate the children by his Spirit and bring them into the covenant of obedience and love for the Lord (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:39).
God will come to be with his people and will transform Zion’s destiny from the darkness as black as night caused by sin and judgment.
The transformation of all nations and mighty kings will be so radical that all kingdoms will take notice and be drawn to God through his people (see also Revelation 21:24).
Zion’s losses from warfare will be restored by the wealth of many lands; foreign nations will be eager to make a contribution (Isaiah 60:11; Isaiah 61:6; Isaiah 66:12; see Revelation 21:26).

Midian and Ephah were Midianite tribes located southeast of Israel. • Sheba was a region in southern Arabia (see 1 Kgs 10:1-2) famed for frankincense (Jeremiah 6:20). • These were real nations—the restoration would be a historical reality, not just an idealistic vision. Many nations would submit themselves to and worship the Lord.

Kedar was a tribe in Arabia (Isaiah 21:16-17). • Nebaioth was an Ishmaelite tribe. • I will make my Temple glorious: The glory of God will be even more evident than it was in Solomon’s Temple (see Isaiah 6:1-5; Haggai 2:9; Revelation 21:11, Revelation 21:22).
filled you with splendor: See Revelation 21:26.
their kings will serve you: God’s people who were previously humiliated (Isaiah 2:11) will be exalted.
Those who previously oppressed the people of God will one day participate in restoring the holy city (see Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 19:18-25; Nehemiah 2:8; Amos 9:12).

There are two likely reasons for why the gates are not closed at night (see also Revelation 21:25): (1) So much traffic will be coming into the city (Isaiah 60:8-10) that the gates will need to be open. (2) The citizens of Zion will no longer need to fear enemies because the Lord is their protector (Isaiah 60:18); the nations that remain will be serving the Lord and his people (Isaiah 60:9, Isaiah 60:12).
In the coming age, nations that refuse to obey God will be destroyed.

The Temple was God’s sanctuary, the symbol of his presence on earth. Believers now are the temple of God by the indwelling Spirit (1 Cor 3:16). We still await the fullness of God’s presence (Revelation 21:22).

beautiful forever, a joy to all generations: This would be radical change from the conditions of the Exile in Babylon. Fulfillments of this prophecy include the Jews’ restoration from exile, the coming of Jesus Christ, and the inclusion of the Gentiles in the church. The final fulfillment awaits the glorious second coming of Jesus Christ, which will usher in the new Jerusalem.

gold . . . silver . . . bronze . . . iron: These metals are for adornment and strength (cp. Isaiah 54:11; Revelation 21:15-21). • Peace and righteousness will bring harmony and blessing among people and with God.
These verses portray Zion’s future grandeur (cp. Revelation 21:10–22:4).

praise will be on the lips of all who enter there (literally they will call your gates “praise”): Entrance into the city of salvation will be through the metaphorical gates of praise to the Lord for his great salvation.
Natural sources of light such as the sun and the moon will be as nothing in comparison to the brightness of God’s presence (see also Isaiah 9:2; Isaiah 30:26; Zechariah 2:5; Revelation 21:23-24).

The citizens of Zion will be righteous, enjoying a right relationship with God and with others (Revelation 21:27). • their land: Or the entire earth (Isaiah 54:5; Isaiah 62:7; Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22).
I, the Lord: The Lord identifies himself as the covenant God of Israel. His identity ensures that he will make it happen (see Isaiah 27:3-4).

The presence of God’s Spirit ensures the success of the servant’s mission (see Isaiah 11:1-5; Isaiah 42:1). • The servant will restore and heal the marginalized poor and the brokenhearted (see Isaiah 25:4).
The servant here proclaims the good news that his ministry will restore Zion. The Lord Jesus applied these words to his own mission (Luke 4:18-19).

The time of the Lord’s favor is the day of God’s salvation (see Isaiah 49:8). • the day of God’s anger: God now turns his wrath against the enemies of his people. It will be a day of righteous vengeance (see Isaiah 34:8; Isaiah 63:3-4).

Putting ashes on one’s head was a sign of mourning (note the reversal of the judgment stated in Isaiah 3:16-25). Mourning would be replaced by joy. The words translated crown of beauty and ashes form a wordplay in Hebrew. • joyous blessing (literally oil of gladness): A face covered with oil was a sign of blessing and well-being (see Psalm 45:8; Psalm 133:2). • The remnant would start out as small offshoots but would grow into great oaks (see Isaiah 60:21).
priests . . . ministers: The nation would fulfill its original calling (Exodus 19:6).
The people had suffered God’s wrath for their sins (Isaiah 40:2); now they would receive a double share of God’s blessing.
Those who belong to the community of God’s people are to imitate the character of God, who loves justice (see Micah 6:8) and hates wrongdoing (Isaiah 33:15).
Their descendants: The covenant will be effective from generation to generation. • The Lord has blessed them in fulfillment of his promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:1-2; see Isaiah 65:23).

clothing of salvation . . . robe of righteousness: With great joy God will clothe his people with the benefits of his salvation and righteousness (see Isaiah 51:5; Isaiah 56:1), like a bridegroom . . . or a bride (see Isaiah 49:18; Isaiah 62:5; Jeremiah 2:32; Jeremiah 7:34; Jeremiah 16:9; Jeremiah 25:10; Jeremiah 33:11).
The servant here commits himself to proclaiming the good news continuously until the glory of Zion is realized.

The real beauty and glory of God’s people would not be seen in earthly treasures or a rebuilt city but would shine forth from their righteousness. Others would be drawn by this divine gift. • A new name reflects the change in Zion’s status (see Isaiah 62:4).

The Forsaken City: In the Exile, the Lord abandoned his people to the judgment they deserved (Isaiah 54:7). • The Bride of God: The people will be “married” to the Lord—an appropriate image for the close covenant relationship (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 1:1–3:5).
The watchmen probably represent the prophets. • they will pray day and night: They will continually seek the full restoration and blessing of Zion, unlike the destructive watchmen of Isaiah 56:10.

The Lord swore an oath just as he did when he had sworn an oath to Noah (Genesis 8:20–9:17), to Abraham (Genesis 22:16; see also Luke 1:73; Hebrews 6:13), and to David (Psalm 89:3). • I will never again hand you over: In order to punish and purge a remnant from his people, God had intentionally brought in the Assyrians and Babylonians to decimate them (see Isaiah 6:12-13). He would never do this again.

The people would eat and drink the fruit of their labor (Isaiah 65:13, Isaiah 65:22; see Leviticus 23:39-40; Deuteronomy 14:22-26). This is the opposite of what happened when God judged them (see Deuteronomy 28:38-40; Amos 5:11; Micah 6:14-15).

highway: See also Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 57:14. • A flag for all the nations to see is a signal that directs foreigners to come to Zion for God’s salvation. Earlier, a similar signal was used to call for the nations to attack Judah (Isaiah 5:26).

This call to prepare for God’s coming salvation combines elements from all parts of Isaiah: the proclamation (the signal or banner, see Isaiah 5:26), the preparation of the road (Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 57:14), the coming of God with his reward (Isaiah 40:5, Isaiah 40:9-10), and the holy and redeemed citizenry (Isaiah 35:8-10).
The Lord’s robes are stained red with blood (Isaiah 63:3; cp. Revelation 19:13). • The name Bozrah (Hebrew botsrah) is a wordplay on the verb batsar (“gather grapes”).
The judgment of Edom typifies God’s judgment of all the nations (see also Isaiah 34:5-15).
The term red (Hebrew ’adom) is a wordplay on the name Edom.
the time . . . to avenge my people: See study note on 34:8. • to ransom: See study note on 43:1.
made them stagger: The wicked nations would be forced to drink from the intoxicating cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 49:26; Isaiah 51:17, Isaiah 51:21).
unfailing love . . . all he has done . . . his great goodness: The whole history of God’s care for his people demonstrates his compassion, provision, and protection.
The prophet reflects on Israel’s past, how God showed his unfailing love and how his people alternatively rebelled against him, suffered hardship, returned to the Lord, and experienced his blessing.

They are my very own people: God’s possession of and commitment to his people was central to the covenant (see Isaiah 43:1). • they will not betray me: The Lord expected his own people to honor their relationship with him, unlike the nations, whose story is a history of treachery (Genesis 3:1–11:32). But Israel, too, betrayed their God (Isaiah 63:10). • their Savior: God rescued and protected his people (see Isaiah 43:3).

he also suffered: God identified with his suffering people, and their suffering brought him grief. Later, Jesus suffered on behalf of all humanity. • and he personally rescued them: e.g., see Exodus 12:25-33; Exodus 14:10-31; Exodus 23:20-23.

But they rebelled: See also Isaiah 1:2, Isaiah 1:4; Isaiah 59:1-15; Psalm 78:1-72, Psalm 106:1-48. • Persistent disobedience and unbelief grieved his Holy Spirit (Psalm 106:33; Matthew 12:32; Mark 3:29). • he became their enemy: Examples include Israel’s period of wandering in the wilderness (see the book of Numbers), the period of the judges (see the book of Judges), and the period leading up to the Exile (see the book of Jeremiah).
God gave his people rest after he brought them into the Promised Land (see Isaiah 63:9; Joshua 1:13; Joshua 22:4; Joshua 23:1).
The prophet’s reflections on the past (Isaiah 63:7-14) inspire him to pray that God would now rescue his people as he has done before.

our Father: God’s fatherhood and his commitment to his children are much more important and secure than national ancestry (see Isaiah 9:6; Isaiah 64:8; Deuteronomy 32:6; Psalm 68:5; Malachi 2:10; Matthew 6:9-15; Romans 8:15-17).

The prophet understands that God has the power to keep his people faithful, so he asks, why have you allowed us to turn from your path? • Return and help us: God likewise has the power to call his people back to himself (Ezekiel 36:25-27) and to defeat all their enemies.
The people were supposed to be holy, but their lack of holiness had led to destruction. • The holy place was the Temple, which the Babylonians destroyed in 586 BC (Isaiah 64:11; 2 Kgs 25:1-21).
Israel was constantly turning from God and then being punished by him.
constant sinners . . . infected and impure with sin: See also Isaiah 59:1-15. The only hope for salvation and transformation is through Jesus Christ (see Romans 7:25–8:11).

you have turned away from us: See Isaiah 1:15; Isaiah 30:20; Isaiah 59:2. • turned us over to our sins: Because the people were so bent on sinning, God left them to perish in their sinful ways (see Romans 1:24).
clay . . . potter: See also Isaiah 29:16; Isaiah 45:9; Romans 9:20-21.
holy cities: All the cities of Judah were considered holy to God. However, the Temple in the host city of Jerusalem was the most holy place.
The Lord opened up every opportunity for the people of Israel to seek him (Isaiah 55:6; Isaiah 58:2), but they did not do so.
Here the Lord responds to the prayer in Isaiah 63:7–64:12.
Sacred gardens were a part of the fertility religion of Baal.

worshiping the dead: God had banned the practice of necromancy (consulting dead spirits; see Isaiah 8:19-22; Isaiah 47:9; Deuteronomy 18:9-11). • the flesh of pigs . . . other forbidden foods: See Isaiah 66:3-4; Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:3, Deuteronomy 14:8.

you will defile me! I am holier than you! The people of Israel used the language of ritual purification, as stated in the laws of Moses, yet they practiced rites influenced by paganism. Because of this hypocrisy, they were a stench in God’s nostrils (see Isaiah 1:10-15).

my decree is written out: God is fully committed to carry out his plan. • The godly had asked whether the Lord would stand silent forever (Isaiah 64:12). God answered that he would not but would deal with the wicked before restoring the righteous remnant.
The people of Israel practiced their pagan religion at sacred shrines on mountains and hills (see 1 Kgs 14:23; Hosea 4:13).
The Lord planned to spare and reward a remnant of righteous people.

Sharon was a fertile and beautiful marshy region southwest of Mount Carmel (see Isaiah 33:9). The valley of Achor in the vicinity of Jericho was associated with the curse on Achan (Joshua 7:24-26); it would be transformed into a place of blessing (Hosea 2:15). These western and eastern regions might represent the renewal of the whole land.
Fate and Destiny are names of pagan gods (Gad, Meni) that were thought to bring fortune and determine one’s destiny.
‘destine’: This verb (Hebrew manithi) is a wordplay on Meni (see study note on 65:11). God alone controls human and national destinies.
The contrast between the wicked (addressed as you) and God’s servants pertains to all areas of life. God punishes the wicked but blesses those who truly serve him (see Isaiah 65:17-25).
The new name given to the faithful represents a new identity and a deeper relationship with the Lord (see also Isaiah 62:2).
evil of earlier days: Cp. Revelation 21:4.

The new heavens and new earth will be a place of righteousness (see also 2 Pet 3:13; Revelation 21:1-27). Paul described those who believe in Christ as already being part of the new creation (see 2 Cor 5:17; Galatians 6:15).
Jerusalem here symbolizes God’s eternal kingdom (Revelation 21:1-4).
God will be present with his people (see also Isaiah 19:22; Isaiah 30:19; cp. Isaiah 1:15; Isaiah 59:2).
The snakes represent evil (Isaiah 27:1; Genesis 3:1-24).

my throne . . . my footstool: God’s kingdom extends over all creation (see Isaiah 40:22; Matthew 5:34-35). • a temple . . . a resting place: Because the entire universe is God’s dwelling place, humans cannot limit him to a building (see 1 Kgs 8:27). • Stephen quoted Isaiah 66:1-2 in his last sermon (Acts 7:49-50).

God is pleased to dwell with those who have humble and contrite hearts (Isaiah 57:15; Psalm 51:17). • who tremble at my word: The humble and contrite submit themselves to God’s will, whereas the arrogant resist it.

delighting in their detestable sins: Literally delighting in abominations, which refers to pagan worship practices. • sacrifice a bull . . . blessed an idol: Wicked people brought sacrifices as prescribed by the law, but their sin rendered those sacrifices equivalent to pagan offerings (see Isaiah 1:11-17).

terrible noise from the Temple: This parallels the situation described in Ezekiel 9:1-11 when God’s executioner began to destroy the wicked people of Jerusalem. • vengeance against his enemies: God would deal out retribution to the disobedient members of his own people. They were his enemies because of their persistent sin and rejection of God.
birth pains . . . gives birth to a son: See Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 54:1-3.
by the time . . . her children will be born: A miraculous repopulation of Zion would occur (see Isaiah 49:19-20; Isaiah 54:1-3; cp. Isaiah 1:8-9).
The Lord promised that he would surely recreate his holy nation.
a river: The people, who lost peace and prosperity in the Exile, would receive it back abundantly (see Isaiah 48:18).
I will comfort you: Cp. Isaiah 40:1.
flourish like the grass: Contrast Isaiah 40:7; Isaiah 64:6. • God’s enemies included the disobedient from the foreign nations and from within Israel (see Isaiah 61:2; Isaiah 66:6).

the Lord is coming with fire: God will appear with furious judgment against his enemies (see Psalm 7:13). By contrast, he will reveal his glory to his people (see Isaiah 40:5, Isaiah 40:10). • God will judge all creation as a part of the process of renewing the earth (see Isaiah 24:1-4; Isaiah 65:17).
Apostates who ‘consecrate’ and ‘purify’ themselves through idolatrous practices are an abomination to God (cp. Isaiah 1:28-31; Isaiah 65:4).

When God reveals his glory to all people, the nations join in God’s plan of redemption; they can even serve as priests and Levites before him. The godly from all nations last from generation to generation as they serve the living God.

The sign is the proclamation of God’s glory among the nations (Isaiah 66:20). God will establish a righteous and faithful new people consisting of godly Gentiles together with faithful Israelites (Revelation 15:3-4; see also Acts 2:1-47).
That some of the Gentiles would serve as priests and Levites signifies the removal of God’s distinction between Hebrews and Gentiles (see Isaiah 56:7; see also Galatians 6:15; Ephesians 4:11-13).

always be my people: God’s promise to Abraham was secure (Genesis 17:7; see also Galatians 3:8, Galatians 3:14). • a name that will never disappear: The identity of this new people will last forever (see Isaiah 59:21).

Isaiah gives a final warning of the severity of God’s judgment. The book begins and ends with the condemnation of those who have rebelled (see Isaiah 1:2-4). • The judgment of God on wicked humans will generate utter horror because such people will have no hope and no relief from suffering (see also Matthew 5:22; Matthew 25:41; Mark 9:47-48; Revelation 20:11-15).
